articles.title: Wound Healing: Pathophysiology
articles.markdown: # Wound Healing: Pathophysiology # Introduction Wound healing involves a series of stages that restore the integrity of the skin or other tissues following injury.  The process helps prevent infection, minimize tissue loss, and ensure proper function of affected areas.  This article focuses on the phases of wound healing and factors affecting healing.  The clinical presentation and management of wounds are described in detail in a separate article. # Phases of wound healing Wound healing can be divided into 4 distinct phases: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling.  These stages overlap and can vary in duration depending on the nature of the wound and the patient's overall health ((Figure 1)). ## Hemostasis (immediate response) - **Timeframe**:  Begins immediately after injury. - **Key events**: - Vasoconstriction occurs to minimize blood loss, followed by platelet aggregation and clotting cascade activation, which lead to platelet plugging, fibrin clot formation, and cessation of bleeding. - Fibrin clot formation acts as a temporary barrier to prevent further bleeding and provides a scaffold for incoming cells. - The clot also releases growth factors (eg, platelet-derived growth factor, transforming growth factor-beta \[TGF-β\]) that initiate the inflammatory phase. ##  Inflammation (response to injury) - **Timeframe**:  Typically lasts 3 hours to 5 days after injury. - **Key events**: - Mast cells degranulate, releasing histamine and other chemical mediators that increase vascular permeability and promote cellular infiltration (eg, neutrophils, monocytes). - Neutrophils, the first immune cells to migrate to the site of injury, digest bacteria, necrotic tissue, and foreign debris. - Monocytes are transformed into macrophages, which secrete growth factors (eg, TGF-β, vascular endothelial growth factor \[VEGF\]) that stimulate the next phase of healing (tissue regeneration) by enhancing angiogenesis and promoting fibroblast proliferation. ## Proliferation (tissue formation) - **Timeframe**:  Begins during the inflammatory phase (3-5 days following injury) and continues for weeks afterward. - **Key events**: - **Angiogenesis**:  Proliferation and migration of endothelial cells from nearby blood vessels lead to ingrowth of new capillaries into the collagen matrix.  The formation of new blood vessels supplies the healing tissue with oxygen and nutrients. - **Fibroplasia**:  Fibroblasts multiply and synthesize ground substance and type III collagen, which form an amorphous gel into which new capillaries can grow.  Fibroblasts also secrete fibroblast growth factor and VEGF, which stimulate endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation, leading to the formation of new capillaries. - **Granulation tissue forms**:  Granulation tissue consists of newly grown capillaries, fibroblasts, and extracellular matrix.  It provides a scaffold for epithelial cell migration and facilitates wound contraction. - **Epithelialization**:  Epithelialization involves the migration and proliferation of basal keratinocytes at the wound edges driven by growth factors (eg, TGF-α).  These factors promote keratinocyte proliferation and migration over the granulation tissue, forming a new epithelial layer that restores the skin's barrier function.  As healing progresses, epithelial cells differentiate into the stratified epidermis, reestablishing the skin's protective barrier. ## Remodeling (maturation and strengthening) - **Timeframe**:  Approximately 3 weeks to 2 years. - **Key events**: - Matrix metalloproteinases secreted by several different cell types (eg, fibroblasts, macrophages, neutrophils, some epithelial cells) facilitate the degradation of collagen and other proteins in the extracellular matrix in a highly regulated fashion.  The type III collagen laid down in a rapid, disorganized manner during the proliferation phase is replaced by type I collagen, now arranged in well-organized, parallel bundles with extensive cross-linking.  This increases tensile strength and decreases the thickness of the scar (ie, flattening). - The wound contracture process reduces the size of the wound, and scar tissue is remodeled, although it does not fully restore the original tissue structure. - The final wound strength is often only 70%-80% of the original skin strength, and scarring is a common result. # Factors affecting wound healing Wound healing is influenced by systemic and local factors that can impair tissue regeneration and lead to delayed healing, chronic wounds, or increased susceptibility to infection. ## Systemic factors - **Advanced age**:  Cellular senescence, reduced fibroblast proliferation, and diminished angiogenic response impair the regenerative capacity of aging skin.  In addition, decreased immune function predisposes elderly individuals to infections. - **Diabetes mellitus**:  Hyperglycemia disrupts leukocyte function, impairs fibroblast activity, and compromises neovascularization, leading to increased infection risk, delayed granulation tissue formation, and chronic ulceration. - **Malnutrition**:  Deficiencies in protein, vitamin C, zinc, and iron hinder collagen synthesis, impair immune responses, and delay reepithelialization.  Hypoalbuminemia specifically reduces oncotic pressure, leading to tissue edema and impaired nutrient transport. - **Immunosuppression**:  Conditions such as HIV and malignancy or corticosteroid therapy blunt the inflammatory response, reducing the recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages necessary for microbial clearance and tissue remodeling. - **Chronic diseases**:  Renal and hepatic dysfunction impair detoxification and metabolic processes essential for collagen synthesis and tissue repair.  Peripheral arterial disease reduces perfusion, limiting oxygen and nutrient delivery to the wound bed. ## Local factors - **Wound infection**:  Bacterial colonization prolongs the inflammatory phase, increases protease activity, and depletes essential growth factors, ultimately delaying healing. - **Hypoxia/ischemia**:  Poor tissue perfusion limits oxygen availability, impairing fibroblast function, angiogenesis, and immune responses. - **Mechanism of injury**:  High-force compression injuries (ie, crush injuries) lead to extensive soft tissue damage, microvascular disruption, and ischemic necrosis.  Bite wounds often introduce polymicrobial infections.  Puncture wounds can introduce pathogens into deeper tissue layers, increasing the risk of abscess formation, osteomyelitis, or tenosynovitis. - **Mechanical stress**:  Excessive tension, shear forces, or repetitive trauma can lead to dehiscence. - **Foreign bodies/necrotic tissue**:  The presence of debris or devitalized tissue acts as a nidus for infection and inflammation, preventing proper reepithelialization and granulation tissue formation. - **Excessive tissue loss**:  Large, full-thickness wounds or traumatic degloving injuries often require skin grafts, flaps, or tissue expansion to achieve adequate closure.  In cases in which primary closure is not feasible, secondary intention healing or delayed closure may be necessary. - **Radiation exposure**:  Prior radiation therapy can induce endothelial damage, reduce vascularity, and impair fibroblast function, leading to delayed healing and increased risk of nonhealing wounds. # Summary Wound healing is a coordinated, overlapping process consisting of hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling.  Immediately after injury, clot formation limits blood loss and establishes a scaffold that initiates inflammation, during which time immune cells clear debris and secrete growth factors.  The proliferative phase rebuilds tissue through angiogenesis, fibroblast activity, granulation tissue formation, and epithelialization, restoring structural integrity.  Remodeling then reorganizes collagen and contracts the wound, increasing tensile strength.  Healing efficiency may be impaired by systemic factors (eg, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, aging) and local conditions (eg, infection, hypoxia, mechanical stress), which can prolong inflammation and disrupt normal tissue repair. ​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌

articles.title: Visual Pathway
articles.markdown: # Visual Pathway # Introduction The visual pathway is the neural system responsible for transmitting visual information from the retina to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.  It is essential for the perception of form, color, motion, and spatial orientation.  Visual processing begins with optical refraction by the cornea and lens, followed by the conversion of light into electrical signals by the retinal photoreceptors.  These signals are then relayed through a series of precisely organized neural structures, including the optic nerves, optic chiasm, optic tracts, lateral geniculate nuclei, optic radiations, and, finally, the visual cortex. # The eye ## Refraction of light Refraction is the bending of light as it passes through media of different optical densities.  It is essential for vision because it allows incoming light rays, which enter the eye from various angles, to be focused precisely onto the retina.  A sharp image is formed only when light converges accurately on the retinal photoreceptors, particularly in the fovea centralis.  Without proper refraction, light scatters and is improperly focused, resulting in a blurred image. The eye has several structures that bend and focus light onto the retina ((Figure 1)): - **Cornea**:  The eye's first and most powerful refractive surface, the cornea is the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye, which has a fixed curvature and contributes approximately 70% of the eye's total refractive power. - **Aqueous humor**:  This clear fluid within the anterior chamber contributes minimally to refraction but helps transmit light between the cornea and lens. - **Lens**:  The second major refractive structure of the eye, the lens has an adjustable curvature that allows for accommodation, the process by which the lens changes its shape to focus on objects at varying distances. - **Near vision**:  Ciliary muscle contracts → zonular fibers relax → lens thickens and becomes more convex → increases refractive power for focusing on near objects. - **Distance vision**:  Ciliary muscle relaxes → zonular fibers tighten → lens flattens → decreases refractive power for distant objects. After light passes through the lens and vitreous compartment, the image created on the retina is inverted and reversed ((Figure 2)).  This means that the temporal (lateral) retinas process images from the nasal (medial) visual field, and the nasal retinas process images from the temporal visual field. ## Refractive errors Visual impairments due to refractive errors include: - **Myopia (nearsightedness)** ((Figure 3)):  Light focuses in front of the retina, causing poor distance vision. - **Hyperopia (farsightedness)** ((Figure 4)):  Light focuses behind the retina, causing poor near vision. - **Astigmatism** ((Figure 5)):  Irregular curvature of the cornea or lens leads to a distorted, blurred image. - **Presbyopia:**  Age-related loss of lens elasticity results in impaired accommodation, especially for near focus (eg, reading). # The retina ## The neural sensor Located at the back of the eye, the retina converts light into electrical signals that are then sent to the brain via the optic nerve.  It contains layers of specialized cells that sequentially process visual information ((Figure 6)). - **Photoreceptors**:  Located in the outermost layer of the retina, photoreceptors hyperpolarize in response to light and modulate downstream neurons. - **Rods**:  Highly sensitive to light; provide night vision and low-resolution, monochromatic (no color) vision.  Rods are concentrated in the peripheral retina. - **Cones**:  Enable daytime and color vision (red, green, blue); responsible for high visual acuity.  Cones are concentrated in the fovea centralis. - **Bipolar cells**:  Transmit signals from photoreceptors to ganglion cells. - **Ganglion cells**:  Receive input from bipolar cells and generate action potentials.  Axons of ganglion cells form the optic nerve. - **Horizontal and amacrine cells**:  Modulate and integrate signals to enhance contrast, motion detection, and spatial resolution. ## Special regions of the retina - **Macula lutea**:  The central area of the retina with a high density of cones; specialized for high-acuity central vision. - **Fovea centralis**:  The center of the macula; a cone-only region with the sharpest visual resolution. - **Optic disc**:  Site where ganglion cell axons converge to form the optic nerve; no rods or cones are present, resulting in a physiologic "blind spot" ((Figure 7)). ## Retinal pathology - **Central retinal artery occlusion**:  Reduction or complete cessation of retinal perfusion leads to retinal ischemia and the sudden onset of painless monocular vision loss. - **Age-related macular degeneration**:  Progressive loss of central vision impairs reading and facial recognition; peripheral vision is preserved. - **Retinal detachment**:  Separation of the neurosensory retina (eg, photoreceptors) from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (which provides oxygen and nutrients) impairs the function of retinal cells, often presenting with flashes of light and floaters.  It can lead to permanent photoreceptor degeneration and vision loss if not corrected. # Neural visual pathway Neural signals travel along the following visual pathway:  Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tracts → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations → primary visual cortex ((Figure 8)).  Lesions along this pathway produce various types of visual deficits based on the location and the nerve fibers that are affected. ## Optic nerve (CN II) - Formed by retinal ganglion cell axons.  Lesions in the optic nerve (eg, central retinal artery occlusion, optic neuritis) cause **monocular blindness (anopia)** ((Figure 9)). ## Optic chiasm - Fibers from the nasal half of the retina (which process the temporal visual field) cross at the optic chiasm, but the temporal retinal fibers (which process the nasal visual fields) remain ipsilateral.  The hemivisual fields of each eye are processed on the contralateral side of the brain (eg, left visual field of the left and right eye is processed in the right hemisphere) ((Figure 10)). - Lesions at the optic chiasm (eg, compression by a pituitary adenoma ((Figure 11))) cause a **bitemporal hemianopia** ((Figure 12)). ## Optic tracts - The optic tracts carry contralateral visual field information from the optic chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus. - Lesions in the optic tract (eg, occlusion of the anterior choroidal artery) cause a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia** (loss of the same visual field in both eyes) ((Figure 13)). ## Lateral geniculate nucleus - The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) is a 6-layered visual relay center within the posterolateral thalamus that sends fibers to the visual cortex via optic radiations. - Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or tumor involving the LGN) cause a **contralateral homonymous visual field deficit**. ## Optic radiations - **Inferior optic radiations**:  Carry information from the superior visual field (inferior retina) through the temporal lobe (Meyer loop) to the visual cortex.  Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or mass involving the temporal lobe) cause a **contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia** ("pie in the sky") ((Figure 14)). - **Superior optic radiations**:  Carry information from the inferior visual field (superior retina) through the parietal lobe to the visual cortex.  Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or mass involving the parietal lobe) cause a **contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia** ("pie on the floor") ((Figure 15)). Large infarctions involving the territory supplied by the middle cerebral artery can damage both the upper and lower limbs of the optic radiations, resulting in homonymous hemianopia. ## Primary visual cortex - Located in the occipital lobe and is retinotopically organized (eg, specific retinal areas map to specific areas of the visual cortex). - Macular vision is processed by the posterior cortex. - Peripheral vision is processed by the anterior cortex. - Lesions in this region (eg, occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery) cause a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing** (the cortical structures responsible for macular vision are dual-supplied from the middle and posterior cerebral arteries). After visual information is received in the occipital cortex, it is relayed along distinct pathways to association cortices for higher-order processing ((Figure 16)).  The ventral (P) pathways project to the occipitotemporal association cortex for the identification of letters, colors, shapes, and faces (ie, what is it?).  The dorsal (M) pathways project to the parietooccipital association cortex for processing of motion and spatial relationships (ie, where is it?). # Summary Vision begins when light is refracted by the cornea and lens and focused onto the retina, where rods and cones convert light into neural signals.  These signals travel via ganglion cells into the optic nerve, cross partially at the optic chiasm, and continue through the optic tracts, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations to reach the primary visual cortex.  Lesions along this pathway produce characteristic visual field defects ((Figure 17)). ​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​

articles.markdown:
# Tumor Suppressor Genes # Introduction Cancer is a heterogeneous disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells that have acquired the ability to evade the body's normal control mechanisms.  The progression from normal cells to this neoplastic state is a multistep process in which cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes, leading to the malignant phenotype. Two key genetic changes seen in almost all cancer cells include inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and activation of proto-oncogenes ((Figure 1)).  These changes contribute to the properties unique to cancer, including: - Loss of growth suppression and resistance to apoptosis via inactivation of tumor suppressor genes. - Sustained cell proliferative signaling and capacity for cell invasion via activation of proto-oncogenes. Identification of these mutations is important, as these alterations can inform cancer risk screening, provide prognostic indicators, and guide selection of specific targeted therapies. # Tumor suppressor genes Tumor suppressor genes protect cells from developing into cancer.  They perform key regulatory functions, such as inhibiting excessive cell division, promoting apoptosis, and repairing damaged DNA.  In most cases, the presence of just 1 active allele is sufficient to maintain these protective roles.  However, when both alleles are inactivated (eg, through genetic mutations), these normal safeguards are no longer present, allowing for uncontrolled cell growth and potential tumor formation (ie, Knudson "2-hit" hypothesis ((Figure 2))). ## *RB1* gene - **Function**:  The *RB1* gene encodes the Rb protein, which integrates signals from various extracellular and intracellular sources to determine whether a cell should proceed through the cell cycle (ie, G1/S checkpoint). - If signals indicate the cell cycle should not proceed (eg, terminally differentiated cell, damaged DNA), the Rb protein stays in its active (ie, dephosphorylated) form.  While active, Rb binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors.  Without E2F, the cell cycle pauses at the G1/S checkpoint, allowing for the cell to repair itself if necessary ((Figure 3)). - If signals indicate the cell cycle can proceed (eg, DNA has been successfully repaired), cyclin-dependent kinases phosphorylate Rb, inactivating it.  Inactivated Rb releases the bound E2F, allowing the cell to proceed through the G1/S checkpoint. - **Mutation**:  One copy of the *RB1* gene is located on each homolog of chromosome 13.  A single functional allele is sufficient to produce enough Rb protein to regulate the G1/S checkpoint.  However, biallelic loss of *RB1* (eg, nonsense mutations, deletions) eliminates this protective function and allows cells to progress through the cell cycle unchecked. - **Associated condition**:  **Retinoblastoma**.  Although the Rb protein serves a tumor suppressor role ubiquitously in all cells, the *RB1* mutation particularly affects the retina.  Because total loss of tumor suppressor function is needed for cancer to develop, retinoblastoma can present in 2 main forms, depending on whether the patient has a germline *RB1* mutation. - Hereditary retinoblastoma:  These patients are born with a germline defect in 1 of the *RB1* genes, meaning every cell in the body already carries the first "hit" needed for tumor development.  Because only 1 additional (somatic) mutation is required to inactivate the remaining normal *RB1* allele, this second "hit" can occur independently in multiple retinal cells.  As a result, an increased risk of bilateral disease exists. - Sporadic retinoblastoma:  These patients lack an underlying germline *RB1* mutation.  In this case, 2 independent somatic mutations must occur within the same retinal cell to inactivate *RB1* and initiate tumor formation.  Because this requires 2 rare, spontaneous mutations in a single cell, tumor development is typically limited to unilateral disease at a later age. ## *APC* gene - **Function**:  The *APC* gene encodes the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) protein, which normally binds and promotes the degradation of beta-catenin.  Beta-catenin is a key component of the Wnt signaling pathway, which regulates essential cell processes (eg, proliferation, differentiation), particularly in intestinal epithelial cell renewal. - **Mutation**:  Various mutations (eg, frameshift, deletion) can cause loss of APC function.  Without functional APC, beta-catenin is not adequately degraded and accumulates in the cell, where it activates transcription factors that promote cell proliferation.  This unchecked signaling drives excessive growth of intestinal crypt epithelial cells. - **Associated conditions**:  Sporadic mutations affecting both alleles can lead to early-onset colorectal cancer.  Patients with an underlying germline mutation in *APC* have **familial adenomatous polyposis**, in which thousands of colon polyps develop; in addition, these patients have early-onset colon carcinoma.  *APC* mutations are also associated with other gastrointestinal malignancies (eg, gastric, pancreatic) and medulloblastoma. ## *BRCA1/BRCA2* genes - **Function**:  The *BRCA1* and *BRCA2* (breast cancer type 1 and breast cancer type 2) genes maintain the integrity of the genome by producing proteins that repair double-stranded DNA breaks via homologous recombination. - **Mutation**:  Loss of function leads to accumulation of unrepaired genetic mutations, which dramatically increases the risk of oncogenesis. - **Associated conditions**:  **Breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer**.  Estrogen-responsive tissue (eg, breast, ovarian) appear to be particularly sensitive to *BRCA1/2* dysfunction, leading to a predominance of cancers in these organs ((Table 1)). ## *TP53* gene - **Function**:  The *TP53* gene, often referred to as the "guardian of the genome," plays a critical role in maintaining genetic integrity.  During the G1 phase of the cell cycle, *TP53* responds to signals of cellular stress and DNA damage.  In response to significant genomic injury, the p53 protein is activated and halts further cell cycle progression, providing time for DNA repair.  If the damage is successfully repaired, the cell may proceed to divide; if the damage is irreparable, p53 initiates apoptosis. - **Mutation**:  Loss of *TP53* function allows cells with damaged DNA to survive and proliferate, contributing to malignant transformation. - **Associated conditions**:  Dysfunctional *TP53* is associated with **Li-Fraumeni syndrome**, a cancer predisposition syndrome in which patients are at significantly increased risk for early-onset development of a wide variety of cancers, including carcinomas (eg, breast, adrenocortical), soft tissue and bone sarcomas, brain tumors, and leukemias. ## *PTEN* gene - **Function**:  The *PTEN* (phosphatase and tensin homolog) gene encodes a phosphatase that negatively regulates both the PI3K/AKT pathway and the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, which are key drivers of cell growth, proliferation, and survival. - **Mutation**:  The loss of *PTEN* function leads to unopposed growth and survival signaling. - **Associated conditions**:  Hamartomatous tumors and **Cowden syndrome**, which has an increased risk for breast, thyroid, endometrial, colorectal, and renal cancer. ## *WT1* gene - **Function**:  The *WT1* gene encodes the WT1 protein, a transcription factor involved in regulating growth and development of the kidneys and gonads.  It functions as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting the transcription of several growth factor–inducible genes, thereby limiting excessive cell proliferation. - **Mutation**:  The loss or inactivation of *WT1* leads to abnormal growth factor expression within renal tissue, driving proliferation. - **Associated condition**:  **Wilms tumor** (nephroblastoma) ((Figure 4)). ## *NF1* gene - **Function**:  The *NF1* gene encodes the protein neurofibromin, which negatively regulates the RAS/MAP kinase signaling pathway.  This pathway controls cell proliferation and differentiation. - **Mutation**:  A mutation in *NF1* results in loss of function in neurofibromin, which leads to increased cell proliferation. - **Associated condition**:  **Neurofibromatosis type 1**.  This condition is characterized by multiple benign neurofibromas, CNS tumors (eg, optic gliomas, pilocytic astrocytomas), soft tissue sarcomas, and neuroblastoma ((Table 2)). ## *NF2* gene - **Function**:  The *NF2* gene encodes the protein merlin, a tumor suppressor protein primarily expressed in neural tissue.  Merlin associates with the plasma membrane and mediates contact inhibition, regulating cell adhesion by stabilizing cell-cell junctions and suppressing proliferative signaling. - **Mutation**:  Loss of merlin function disrupts contact inhibition, leading to abnormal cell proliferation. - **Associated condition**:  ***NF2*\-related schwannomatosis**, which is classically associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.  Additional features include intracranial meningiomas and ependymomas ((Table 3)). ## *VHL* gene - **Function**:  The *VHL* gene encodes a protein, von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) ubiquitin ligase, that polyubiquitinates hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), targeting them for degradation.  HIFs play a key role in oxygen sensing and angiogenesis ((Figure 5)). - **Mutation**:  *VHL* mutations (eg, deletion, nonsense, frameshift) disrupt normal HIF degradation, leading to HIF accumulation.  This condition results in overexpression of angiogenic growth factors (eg, VEG-F, PDG-F) and erythropoietin, driving abnormal blood vessel proliferation that can lead to highly vascular tumors and cysts. - **Associated condition**:  VHL disease, which can cause CNS hemangioblastomas, retinal hemangioblastomas, renal clear cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts, and endolymphatic sac tumors of the middle ear ((Table 4)). # Summary Cancer development involves a multistep progression in which cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes leading to the malignant phenotype.  Almost all cancer cells characteristically have 2 key genetic drivers: biallelic inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and/or gain-of-function of proto-oncogenes.  These changes contribute to the properties unique to cancer, such as the loss of growth suppression and resistance to apoptosis via inactivation of tumor suppressor genes, and sustained cell proliferative signaling and capacity for cell invasion via activation of proto-oncogenes. ​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌

articles.title: Thyroid Physiology And Diagnostic Testing
articles.markdown: # Thyroid Physiology And Diagnostic Testing # Introduction The thyroid is a small endocrine gland that plays an important role in regulating the basal metabolic rate.  Thyroid disorders are very common globally and can include hyperthyroidism (overproduction of thyroid hormone), hypothyroidism (underproduction of hormone), and a variety of neoplastic and inflammatory conditions. # Embryology The thyroid is primarily an endodermal derivative.  In utero, the thyroid gland forms from an outpouching of pharyngeal epithelium at the base of the tongue ((Figure 1)).  It then descends to the base of the anterior neck via the thyroglossal duct, which extends from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to the superior midline border of the thyroid ((Figure 2)).  Normally, the duct then atrophies.  Occasionally, failure of normal migration can leave residual deposits of ectopic thyroid tissue along the route of descent, and residual patency of the duct can manifest as a thyroglossal duct cyst. As the cells migrate to the lower neck, they also fuse with parafollicular C cells from the ultimobranchial body of the 4th pharyngeal arch to form the mature thyroid glandular structure ((Figure 3)). # Anatomy The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland that sits on the midline in the lower neck, anterior to the trachea and inferior to the thyroid cartilage ((Figure 4)).  It is composed of 2 lobes with a central isthmus; most patients have a posterior extension from each lobe (tubercle of Zuckerkandl).  The gland is supported by the trachea via the lateral suspensory ligament and is typically mobile, rising with the thyroid cartilage during swallowing.  The parathyroids are a set (usually 4) of small glands that lie immediately posterior to the thyroid lobes. Blood supply to the thyroid is primarily via the paired superior and inferior thyroidal arteries ((Figure 5)).  Innervation to the thyroid is scant, primarily consisting of small sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers that regulate blood flow to the thyroid.  However, the recurrent laryngeal nerve passes through the thyroid, and the superior laryngeal nerve runs in close proximity; these nerves can be injured during thyroid dissection or thyroidectomy. The fundamental unit of thyroid microanatomy is the thyroid follicle ((Figure 6)), spherical structures consisting of a core of glycoprotein colloid, which serves as substrate for synthesis of thyroid hormone, surrounded by cuboidal epithelium.  The reticular tissue between follicles is highly vascular with a dense network of capillaries.  The interfollicular space also contains the parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin. # Thyroid hormone physiology Synthesis of thyroid hormone begins with thyroglobulin, a large glycoprotein produced in thyroid follicular cells and secreted into the follicular lumen ((Figure 7)).  The follicular cells also transport inorganic iodide from the bloodstream into the lumen.  There, thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidizes iodide to iodine, and covalently links it to tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin (ie, organification), forming mono- and diiodotyrosine.  TPO then couples the iodinated tyrosine residues to form triiodothyronine (T3) and tetraiodothyronine (T4, also referred to as thyroxine), which are collectively termed thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormone is stored in the thyroid follicles while still bound to thyroglobulin.  In preparation for release, it is taken up into follicular cells, liberated from thyroglobulin by proteolytic enzymes, and transported into the follicular capillaries.  Most thyroid hormone is released in the form of T4, with only a small amount of T3 released.  T3 (the more active form of thyroid hormone) is then produced by deiodination of T4 in peripheral tissues.  Most thyroid hormone in circulation is bound to plasma proteins, primarily thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, and albumin.  A much smaller free thyroid hormone pool is metabolically active. Thyroid hormone acts on an intranuclear receptor that is ubiquitous in tissues throughout the body.  It acts to stimulate the basal metabolic rate, increasing energy consumption and thermogenesis.  It also increases expression of catecholamine receptors, amplifying adrenergic effects. # Regulation of thyroid endocrine function Thyroid hormone synthesis and release are regulated primarily by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which is secreted by thyrotroph cells of the anterior pituitary ((Figure 8)).  Release of TSH is stimulated in turn by thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus.  Production of both TRH and TSH is suppressed by negative feedback from thyroid hormone. In addition to T4 and T3, a small amount of thyroid hormone is released as reverse T3 (rT3), an inactive isomer.  Conversion of T4 to rT3 also occurs in peripheral tissues; increased rT3 conversion, as can occur in severe illness, leaves less T4 available for deiodination to active T3, which serves as a secondary check on thyroid hormone status. # Effect of pregnancy Pregnancy requires increased thyroid hormone production to meet metabolic demands.  Alterations to thyroid hormone levels occur through 2 primary mechanisms: - Estrogen stimulates the synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) and decreases TBG clearance, leading to higher circulating TBG levels and an increased pool of bound thyroid hormone.  T4 production subsequently increases to maintain free hormone levels ((Figure 9)). - hCG (which shares a common alpha subunit with TSH and a similar beta subunit) directly stimulates thyrotropin receptors on thyroid follicular cells, resulting in increased T4 production.  TSH levels typically fall due to negative feedback of thyroid hormone on pituitary TSH release. # Laboratory testing ## TSH Serum TSH is the primary laboratory test used in diagnosis and management of thyroid conditions.  Abnormalities include the following: - TSH is increased in primary hypothyroidism, central/secondary hyperthyroidism, and under-replacement in thyroid hormone therapy. - TSH is decreased/suppressed in primary hyperthyroidism, central hypothyroidism, and over-replacement in thyroid hormone therapy. Because the pituitary response to changes in thyroid physiologic status is rapid and vigorous, TSH is generally the most sensitive marker in thyroid disease, with levels rising or falling before thyroid hormone levels are outside their laboratory reference ranges.  The correlation between serum TSH and thyroid metabolic status is logarithmic, with changes at the lower end of the reference range representing a greater change in status than a proportional change at the upper end of the range. ## Thyroxine (T4), free and total The bulk of circulating thyroid hormone is in the form of T4.  Levels are elevated in primary and central hyperthyroidism, and decreased in primary and central hypothyroidism.  Because free T4 is the metabolically active fraction and is less affected by plasma binding protein levels, many experts prefer free T4 over total T4 measurement for clinical decision making. ## Triiodothyronine (T3) Serum T3 is often used in evaluation of hyperthyroidism; elevated levels serve to confirm an elevated T4 measurement.  However, TSH, which is elevated in primary hypothyroidism, increases the share of thyroid hormone released as T3, and serum T3 levels are often normal in mild to moderate hypothyroid states.  Therefore, T3 is not recommended in evaluation of hypothyroidism. ## Thyroglobulin A small amount of thyroglobulin is released with thyroid hormone from thyroid follicular cells.  Excessive thyroid hormone production in hyperthyroidism (eg, Graves disease) is typically associated with elevated serum levels of thyroglobulin.  Thyroglobulin levels can be strikingly elevated when hyperthyroidism is due to destruction of thyroid follicles with release of preformed thyroid hormone (eg, painless thyroiditis, subacute \[granulomatous\] thyroiditis).  Also, because thyroglobulin is made exclusively in the thyroid, patients who undergo total thyroidectomy (eg, for thyroid cancer) should have no detectable thyroglobulin in circulation; measurable levels suggest the presence of residual or recurrent neoplastic tissue. ## Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies (Anti-TPO) Anti-TPO is classically used as a marker for chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis and related conditions (eg, painless and postpartum thyroiditis).  In these disorders, high anti-TPO levels are associated with increased risk for progression of subclinical hypothyroidism (ie, elevated TSH with normal free T4 levels) to overt hypothyroidism.  Anti-TPO is not specific to these disorders, however, and also can be seen in Graves disease and other autoimmune endocrinopathies. ## Thyrotropin (TSH) receptor antibodies (TRAb) Autoantibodies against the TSH receptor can activate the receptor independent of TSH (ie, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin).  These antibodies are the hallmark of Graves disease and are a sensitive marker for diagnosis. # Imaging ## Ultrasound Because the thyroid occupies a relatively superficial position in the anterior neck, it is readily accessible to ultrasound imaging.  Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice in evaluating thyroid nodules, and ultrasound characteristics (eg, size, echotexture, calcification) can be used to determine the risk for malignancy and need for tissue sampling.  Ultrasound is also commonly used to guide fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid. Ultrasound with Doppler can assess blood flow in the thyroid, which correlates roughly with metabolic activity and can clarify the differential diagnosis in hyperthyroidism.  Graves disease, which is characterized by increased thyroid hormone synthesis, typically shows increased blood flow; destructive thyroiditis, which causes release of preformed hormone with decreased new hormone synthesis, shows decreased flow.  Thyroid scintigraphy (see below) is usually preferred for this purpose but is contraindicated in pregnant women, in whom ultrasound is preferred. ## Nuclear medicine Radioactive iodine uptake scintigraphy is widely used in the evaluation of hyperthyroidism.  This imaging modality uses a radioiodine tracer to assess uptake and organification of iodine in the thyroid.  Typical patterns include the following: - Diffusely increased uptake ((Image 1)) throughout the thyroid gland suggests Graves disease. - Focal uptake ((Image 2)) with decreased uptake in the remainder of the gland suggests hypermetabolic thyroid nodules (toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter). - Decreased uptake ((Image 3)) throughout the gland suggests destructive thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone intake. # Summary The thyroid gland synthesizes hormones that regulate the body's metabolic rate.  These hormones are produced through a multi-step process that utilizes iodine, and their release is controlled via a feedback loop involving the pituitary gland.  Thyroid-stimulating hormone, produced by the pituitary, is the primary screening tool for diagnosing thyroid conditions.  Imaging techniques such as ultrasound and radioactive iodine uptake scans can further pinpoint the cause of the thyroid dysfunction, such as Graves disease or thyroid nodules. ​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​

articles.title: The Menstrual Cycle
articles.markdown: # The Menstrual Cycle # Introduction The menstrual cycle involves a complex interplay of hormones controlled by the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis to regulate the ovary and uterine endometrium.  The menstrual cycle is approximately 28 days in length and consists of 2 main phases—follicular and luteal—separated by ovulation. # Hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis The HPO axis is the central regulatory system of the menstrual cycle and consists of the following components ((Figure 1)): - Hypothalamus:  Releases pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which stimulates the anterior pituitary gland. - Anterior pituitary gland:  Releases gonadotropins (follicle-stimulating hormone \[FSH\], luteinizing hormone \[LH\]) in response to GnRH. - Ovary:  Responds to FSH by initiating follicular development, which produces estradiol through follicular steroidogenesis. # Follicular phase (days 1-14) The follicular phase begins on the first day of menstruation ((Figure 2)).  The primary objectives of the follicular phase are to create a dominant follicle (ie, ovarian follicular phase) and a thickened endometrium (ie, endometrial proliferative phase) conducive to embryo implantation.  Therefore, the ovarian **follicular phase**, which is **estrogen driven**, directly corresponds to the **endometrial proliferative phase**. During the follicular phase: - FSH levels are initially high (in response to pulsatile GnRH release from the hypothalamus) while LH levels are initially low.  Estrogen and progesterone levels are at their lowest points within the menstrual cycle. - Within the ovary, FSH recruits a cohort of primary follicles that, with maturation, secrete estradiol through steroid synthesis in the surrounding theca and granulosa cells ((Figure 3)).  A dominant follicle is selected by day 7 of the menstrual cycle and begins to grow rapidly while the other follicles undergo apoptosis. - Rising estradiol levels drive endometrial mitosis, proliferation, and stromal vascularization ((Image 1)), resulting in a thickened proliferative endometrium. - Estradiol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland to inhibit further FSH release, thereby preventing the continual recruitment of follicles. # Ovulation (day 14) Ovulation marks the midpoint of the cycle, or the transition between the follicular and luteal phases.  At the midpoint of the cycle, rising estradiol levels cause a unique neuroendocrine phenomenon in which negative feedback changes to positive feedback, resulting in the **LH surge**.  This surge triggers ovulation, or the release of one mature oocyte from the dominant follicle within the ovary. # Luteal phase (days 15-28) Following ovulation, the luteal phase begins, and FSH and LH levels rapidly decline.  Within the ovary, the follicular remnant luteinizes and begins to secrete increasing levels of progesterone.  At the endometrium, the rising progesterone levels induce secretory endometrial changes, which include spiral vessel coiling and large intracytoplasmic glycogen vacuole deposition within the endometrial cells.  Therefore, the **ovarian luteal phase** (which is progesterone driven) directly corresponds to the **endometrial secretory phase** ((Image 2)). If an embryo implants within the endometrium, β-hCG is secreted and sustains the corpus luteum.  Without this pregnancy hormone, the corpus luteum degrades, progesterone declines, and the endometrium sheds.  As progesterone levels fall, FSH levels gradually rise to begin the cycle again. In women with normal, ovulatory menstrual cycles, the luteal phase is consistently 14 days in length.  Any variations in cycle length occur due to variability of the length of the follicular phase. # Summary The normal menstrual cycle is a dynamic and finely regulated process involving intricate histologic changes within the ovaries and endometrium.  The balance of hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian hormones coordinates these events through complex feedback loops to produce one mature oocyte and an endometrium conducive to implantation. ​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌

articles.markdown:
# Renal Anatomy And Physiology # Introduction The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs responsible for maintaining systemic homeostasis.  Their key functions include filtration and waste excretion, sodium and water balance, electrolyte and acid-base handling, and various endocrine roles (eg, vitamin D activation).  This review explores structural and functional characteristics of the kidney, from its embryologic development to the molecular mechanisms underlying filtration and reabsorption.  Endocrine functions are discussed in separate articles. # Embryology and gross morphology ## Embryology The definitive kidney, or metanephros, originates from the intermediate mesoderm.  Its development proceeds through a series of stages (pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros) during the fourth week of embryologic development.  The metanephros arises from the reciprocal interaction between the ureteric bud (which forms the collecting system) and the metanephric mesenchyme (which differentiates into nephrons) ((Figure 1)). ## Gross morphology Each adult kidney sits within the retroperitoneal space ((Figure 2)), shielded by a fibrous renal capsule and surrounded by perirenal fat.  This fatty cushion provides both mechanical protection and thermal insulation.  Each kidney receives blood flow from its respective renal artery and is drained by the renal veins.  The left renal vein is longer, making the left kidney preferred for renal transplant because the greater length simplifies the surgical procedure ((Figure 3)). Internally, the kidney can be divided into 2 primary regions ((Figure 4)): - **Renal cortex**:  This outer granular layer contains glomeruli and most metabolically active regions of the nephron (eg, early proximal tubule) with a rich vascular network. - **Renal medulla**:  This inner region contains renal pyramids and houses the loops of Henle, vasa recta, and collecting ducts.  Each pyramid terminates at a renal papilla, which projects into a minor calyx.  The renal papillae serve as the exit points where collecting ducts converge to drain urine into the minor calyces, which join to form major calyces that in turn converge into the renal pelvis. Some individuals are born with a solitary functioning kidney, as in the case of unilateral renal agenesis (failure of the ureteric bud to develop).  Although most of these people remain asymptomatic due to compensatory hyperfiltration by the remaining kidney, they face an elevated risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to hyperfiltration injury. # The nephron The nephron is the fundamental functional unit of the kidney, responsible for transforming filtered blood (the filtrate) into urine ((Figure 5)).  Each kidney contains approximately 1 million nephrons, each of which consists of a renal corpuscle (site of filtrate formation) and tubule (site of filtrate refinement). ## Renal corpuscle: Filtrate formation The renal corpuscle forms the kidney's filtration apparatus ((Figure 6)) and consists of: - **Glomerulus**:  A specialized capillary network supplied by the afferent arteriole. - **Bowman capsule**:  A double-walled epithelial structure enclosing the glomerulus, consisting of simple squamous epithelium (parietal layer) and specialized podocytes with interdigitating foot processes connected by slit diaphragms (visceral layer) interspersed by proteins (eg, nephrin, podocin). Within the renal corpuscle, blood is filtered through the glomerular capillaries into the Bowman space (confined space within the capsule), forming the filtrate that ultimately becomes urine.  The filtration occurs across the **glomerular filtration barrier**, which progressively increases in selectivity (based on particle size) as substances pass through its 3 layers: - **Fenestrated endothelium**:  Fenestrated endothelium forms the innermost layer of the glomerular capillaries, permitting the passage of many plasma components through pores (70-100 nm in diameter).  Fluid, dissolved solutes, and plasma proteins are allowed through, whereas blood cells are not. - **Glomerular basement membrane (GBM)**:  This middle layer is composed of type IV collagen and heparan sulfate, serving as the most significant physical barrier.  The GBM prevents entry of molecules >40-50 nm. - **Podocyte foot processes**:  These processes form the outermost layer and contain small slit diaphragms (25-60 nm in diameter) that restrict the passage of proteins larger than approximately 70 kDa. In addition to the size barriers, **negatively charged glycoproteins** in all 3 layers add an electrostatic filter that repels larger, negatively charged solutes (eg, albumin) while not affecting small solutes (eg, electrolytes).  This intricate filtration system comprising physical and electrochemical barriers ensures that essential plasma proteins remain in circulation while waste products, electrolytes, and excess fluid are filtered ((Figure 7)). ## Renal tubules: Filtrate refinement Once the glomerular filtrate is formed, it enters the tubular system, where its composition is adjusted through tubular reabsorption (movement of substances from tubular lumen to blood) and secretion (movement from blood to tubular lumen).  The result—the net sum of filtration, reabsorption, and secretion—is excretion, the forming of the final urine.  The functionally distinct tubular segments include: - **Proximal convoluted tubule** (PCT) - Lined by cuboidal epithelial cells with a prominent brush border and abundant mitochondria, optimizing it for extensive solute reabsorption. - Reabsorbs 65%-70% of filtered Na⁺ (eg, via Na+/H+ exchangers), in addition to glucose (via sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 \[SGLT-2\] ((Figure 8))), bicarbonate ((Figure 9)), phosphate (regulated by parathyroid hormone), and Ca2+. - Secretes organic anions (eg, penicillin) via organic anion transporters and reabsorbs uric acid.  Both functions are inhibited by probenecid, a gout medication with a uricosuric effect (probenecid should be avoided in patients taking penicillin) ((figure 10)). - Renal glucose handling follows a titration curve:  At plasma glucose <200 mg/dL, nearly all filtered glucose is reabsorbed.  Beyond the transport maximum, excess glucose spills into urine (glucosuria) ((Figure 11)). - **Loop of Henle** - Descending limb:  Passively reabsorbs water, concentrating tubular fluid. - Thick ascending limb (TAL):  Impermeable to water, it actively transports Na+, K+, and Cl− into the medullary interstitium via Na+\-K+\-2Cl− cotransporters.  This creates a medullary concentration gradient, allowing water reabsorption and urine concentration (discussed later). - Reabsorbs Mg2+ and Ca2+ via paracellular pathways. - **Distal convoluted tubule** (DCT) - This segment adjusts sodium and calcium concentrations (eg, via Na+\-Cl− cotransporters) under regulation by parathyroid hormone. - **Collecting duct** (CD) - The nephron's final segment, the CD, determines urine concentration and composition. - Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) regulates water reabsorption via aquaporin-2 channels, concentrating urine when present and allowing dilution in its absence ((figure 12)). - Principal cells secrete K+ (via ROMK channels) and reabsorb Na+ (via ENaC), modulated by aldosterone.  Intercalated cells maintain acid-base balance by secreting H+ (via H+\-ATPase) and modulating bicarbonate transport.  Both are regulated by aldosterone ((figure 13)). - Urea passively diffuses out of the inner medullary CD, contributing to the medullary osmotic gradient. The following is a summary of electrolyte handling through the tubular segments: - Sodium:  Reabsorbed in PCT (65%), TAL (25%), and DCT/CD (10%). - Potassium:  Reabsorbed in PCT/TAL; secreted in CD (regulated by aldosterone). - Phosphate:  Reabsorbed in PCT (inhibited by parathyroid hormone). - Calcium:  Reabsorbed in PCT (60%), TAL (20%), and DCT (20%). - Magnesium:  Primarily reabsorbed in TAL (70%). There are 2 types of nephrons specialized for different purposes.  **Cortical nephrons** make up the majority of nephrons and are optimized for solute reabsorption (ie, contain short loops of Henle) into peritubular capillaries.  **Juxtamedullary nephrons** extend deep into the medulla and are therefore critical for concentrating urine through the countercurrent multiplication system. The countercurrent multiplication system ((Figure 14)) establishes a **medullary concentration gradient** in the renal medulla to facilitate water reabsorption.  It relies on the unique structure of the loop of Henle.  The descending limb is permeable to water but not solutes; this allows water to leave the tubules, increasing tubular fluid osmolarity.  In contrast, the ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively transports sodium, potassium, and chloride into the medullary interstitium, reducing tubular fluid osmolarity while increasing medullary solute concentration.  This countercurrent flow amplifies the osmotic gradient, which is essential for the CD to reabsorb water under the influence of ADH, ultimately concentrating the urine.  The vasa recta, a specialized capillary network, helps maintain this gradient by preventing the washout of solutes from the medulla. # Vascular architecture Blood enters the kidneys via the renal artery, which divides into interlobar arteries, then arcuate arteries, and, finally, cortical radial arteries.  These give rise to afferent arterioles, forming the glomerular capillary network.  After blood is filtered through the glomerulus, it exits via the efferent arterioles, forming peritubular capillaries (in cortical nephrons) or the vasa recta (in juxtamedullary nephrons) ((Figure 15)).  The blood is finally collected from the peritubular network into cortical radial veins, which coalesce into arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, and, finally, the renal vein. The renal cortex receives approximately 90%-95% of renal blood flow, whereas the renal medulla receives the remaining 5%-10%.  This makes the medulla very sensitive to hypoxia, as demonstrated by the injury pattern seen in ischemic acute tubular necrosis, with the outer medullary cells being most affected ((Figure 16)). # Glomerular filtration ## Net filtration pressure The net filtration pressure, which governs fluid movement across the glomerular filtration barrier, is a result of pressure gradients formed by Starling forces and is calculated by subtracting the oncotic pressure gradient from the hydrostatic pressure gradient (ie, net filtration pressure = \[Pc − Pi\] − \[πc − πi\]) ((Figure 17)): - The hydrostatic pressure gradient (Pc − Pi) is the difference between the hydrostatic pressures in the intraglomerular capillaries and the Bowman space.  Hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries is higher than that in the Bowman space and provides the driving force for fluid efflux from the capillaries. - The oncotic pressure gradient (πc − πi) is the difference between the oncotic pressures in the intraglomerular capillaries and the Bowman space.  Oncotic pressure is driven chiefly by large plasma proteins (eg, albumin), which do not freely filter across the glomerular capillary basement membrane due to both size and charge barriers.  The high oncotic pressure in the capillaries counteracts the capillary hydrostatic pressure and decreases net fluid efflux from the capillaries. ## Renal clearance and renal plasma flow Renal **clearance** is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a given substance by the kidneys per unit time (usually expressed in mL/min).  It reflects the kidney's efficiency in removing a substance from the bloodstream.  Renal clearance of any substance (S) can be calculated as:

Clearance = (\[Urine concentration of S\] × \[Urine flow rate\]) / (Plasma concentration of S)

Renal clearance can vary from 0 to >600 mL/min, depending on the substance.  For example, under normal physiologic conditions, clearance of albumin and glucose is 0 (albumin is not filtered; glucose is filtered and then completely reabsorbed).  In contrast, maximum clearance is demonstrated by **para-aminohippurate** (PAH), which is freely filtered in the glomerulus and also actively secreted in the proximal tubule (ie, tubular fluid concentration increases along the nephron segments ((Figure 18))).  PAH is nearly completely cleared in 1 renal pass, and its clearance therefore approximates the **renal plasma flow** (RPF), which is the volume of plasma passing through the kidney per unit of time (approximately 625 mL/min). In contrast to PAH clearance, inulin clearance, described in the next section, is the gold standard for measuring the glomerular filtration rate ((Figure 19)). ## Glomerular filtration rate The **glomerular filtration rate** (GFR) represents the volume of plasma filtered per minute, typically 90-120 mL/min in healthy adults.  GFR represents the sum of filtration rates across all nephrons and is most accurately measured through **inulin clearance**.  Inulin, an exogenous substance, is an ideal marker because it is freely filtered by the glomerulus and not reabsorbed, secreted, or metabolized by the renal tubules.  As a result, the amount of filtered inulin exactly equals the amount excreted in urine.  However, this method is labor intensive, requiring continuous infusion and multiple blood and urine samples, limiting its clinical use. In clinical practice, GFR is typically estimated using the serum concentration of **creatinine**, a waste product generated during muscle metabolism of creatine.  Creatinine is produced at a relatively constant rate proportional to muscle mass and is freely filtered by the glomerulus without being reabsorbed (and is only slightly secreted).  The **estimated GFR** (eGFR) is calculated using formulas (eg, CKD-EPI, MDRD) that incorporate serum creatinine alongside variables such as age, sex, and race. The relationship between serum creatinine and GFR is nonlinear.  A useful clinical rule is that each 50% reduction in GFR correlates with a doubling of serum creatinine.  For example, if a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL corresponds to a GFR of 100 mL/min, a decline in GFR to 50 mL/min raises serum creatinine to 2.0 mg/dL.  Further reductions to 25, 12.5, and 6.25 mL/min would yield serum creatinine levels of 4.0, 8.0, and 16.0 mg/dL, respectively.  This curvilinear relationship means that in early kidney disease even minor increases in serum creatinine reflect substantial declines in GFR ((Figure 20)).  Consequently, serum creatinine alone is an insensitive marker for detecting early CKD, underscoring why GFR—rather than creatinine concentration alone—is used for CKD staging and management. ## Creatinine clearance Alternatively, **creatinine clearance** (CrCl) provides another approximation of GFR.  CrCl can be measured directly using a 24-hour urine creatinine collection or estimated using the Cockcroft-Gault formula (which incorporates age, weight, sex, and serum creatinine).  However, unlike inulin, a small fraction of creatinine is actively secreted by the proximal tubules, leading to an overestimation of GFR by approximately 10%-20% when using uncorrected CrCl.  Although this overestimation makes CrCl less suitable for precise CKD diagnosis and staging, it remains widely used for medication dosing adjustments because drug dosing studies and guidelines were historically developed using CrCl measurements. ## Advanced biomarkers Given that both eGFR and CrCl rely on serum creatinine, both have limitations in individuals with low muscle mass (eg, malnutrition, lower extremity amputation) or high- or low-protein diets.  In such cases, advanced biomarkers are helpful.  For instance, cystatin C, a small protein produced by all nucleated cells (ie, not affected by muscle mass or dietary protein) and freely filtered by the glomerulus, offers a more reliable biomarker. # Renal hemodynamics ## Renal blood flow and filtration fraction RPF (approximated by PAH clearance) can be used to calculate the following: - Renal blood flow (RBF):  Defined as the volume of whole blood (plasma plus blood cells) passing through the kidneys per unit time.  RBF = RPF/(1 − hematocrit).  RBF reflects overall renal perfusion (approximately 25% of cardiac output, or 1.25 L/min) and is influenced by systemic hemodynamics (eg, blood pressure, vascular resistance). - Filtration fraction (FF):  Expressed as the ratio of GFR to RPF.  It is the portion of RPF that is filtered across the glomerular capillaries.  Normally, FF is approximately 20%, meaning that 20% of the RBF is filtered.  The remaining 80% of the RBF exits the efferent arterioles and joins the peritubular capillary blood flood. ## Mechanisms regulating GFR and RBF Both GFR and RBF are influenced by the vascular tone of both the afferent and the efferent arterioles, as shown in the following table ((Table 1)). # Juxtaglomerular apparatus The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is a specialized structure located where the DCT contacts the afferent and efferent arterioles ((Figure 21)).  The JGA is critical for regulating RBF and glomerular filtration and consists of the following components: - **Macula densa**:  Chemoreceptor cells that sense sodium chloride (NaCl) concentration in the tubular fluid via Na+\-K+\-2Cl− transporters. - **Juxtaglomerular cells**:  Modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin in response to decreased blood pressure, reduced NaCl, or sympathetic stimulation. - **Extraglomerular mesangial cells**:  Cells that facilitate communication within the JGA through gap junctions, fine-tuning the feedback response. In addition to regulating RBF and GFR (discussed in the next section), the JGA also plays a key role in the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system** (RAAS) by releasing renin in response to a variety of renal stimuli, including reduced afferent arteriolar pressure, reduced sodium delivery, and increased sympathetic drive.  Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II by ACE.  Angiotensin II causes systemic vasoconstriction (increasing blood pressure), promotes aldosterone release (increasing blood volume), and stimulates thirst ((Figure 22)). # Regulation of renal blood flow ## Normal renal autoregulation Normally, the kidneys maintain **stable RBF and GFR** over a wide range of mean arterial pressures (MAPs) (80-180 mm Hg) ((Figure 23)).  This process, called renal autoregulation, is accomplished through dynamic adjustments in **afferent arteriole** resistance via the following mechanisms: - **Myogenic response**:  Rising arterial pressure stretches afferent arteriolar smooth muscle, triggering vasoconstriction (through opening of stretch-activated calcium channels).  This reduces blood flow into the glomerulus, preventing abrupt increases in glomerular pressure.  Conversely, dropping arterial pressure triggers afferent vasodilation, increasing RBF (and hence GFR). - **Tubuloglomerular feedback**:  Increased arterial pressure leads to higher filtration of NaCl, which is delivered to the macula densa.  This triggers the paracrine release of vasoconstrictors (eg, adenosine), causing afferent arteriole constriction to limit blood flow.  In contrast, as pressures drop, reduced NaCl delivery releases vasodilators (eg, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) to maintain RBF and GFR. ## Failure of renal autoregulation Under extreme deviations in MAP (<80 mm Hg or >180 mm Hg), renal blood flow autoregulation is unable to maintain stable RBF and GFR, as demonstrated in the following scenarios: - ↓↓ **MAP**:  Autoregulatory vasodilation is overwhelmed, unable to sufficiently elevate RBF and GFR.  Although compensatory prostaglandins (eg, prostaglandin E₂) dilate the afferent arteriole to preserve GFR, prolonged/severe hypotension exhausts this safeguard, causing prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI). - ↑↑ **MAP**:  Excessive pressure overwhelms autoregulatory vasoconstriction, exposing glomeruli to systemic hypertension.  This leads to hyperfiltration, glomerular damage, proteinuria, and inflammation (due to mesangial stretch), culminating in acute hypertensive nephrosclerosis. ## Clinical applications In addition to extreme MAP deviations, renal autoregulation can be disrupted in various clinical scenarios, including: - ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs):  These inhibit angiotensin II, which normally maintains GFR via efferent constriction during reduced MAP (eg, volume depletion).  As MAP decreases, patients on these drugs are prone to prerenal AKI due to afferent vasodilation ((Figure 24)).  However, in patients whose volume status is stable, these medications protect glomerular capillaries (eg, diabetic nephropathy) by reducing intraglomerular hypertension, slowing disease progression despite a minor GFR decline. - NSAIDs:  By inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis (eg, PGE₂), these medications prevent afferent arteriole dilation during hypoperfusion.  In states of low effective arterial blood volume (EABV) (eg, volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis), this causes unopposed vasoconstriction and AKI ((Figure 25)). - SGLT-2 inhibitors:  Blocking SGLT-2 in the proximal tubule reduces glucose and sodium reabsorption, increasing solute delivery to the macula densa.  This enhances tubuloglomerular feedback, causing afferent vasoconstriction, lowering intraglomerular pressure, and reducing hyperfiltration ((Figure 26)).  This renoprotective effect mimics those of ACE inhibitors and ARBs but targets afferent (rather than efferent) arterioles. - Nephrotoxic agents:  Intraarterial iodinated contrast may cause AKI via afferent vasoconstriction (and direct tubular toxicity), especially in CKD.  Calcineurin inhibitors (eg, tacrolimus) can also induce afferent vasoconstriction. - Hepatorenal syndrome:  Advanced cirrhosis leads to severe splanchnic vasodilation and reduced EABV.  Compensatory RAAS hyperactivity (from renal hypoperfusion) causes intense renal vasoconstriction, overwhelming autoregulatory mechanisms and impairing renal function. Beyond these acute disruptions, chronic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus also significantly impact renal autoregulation.  In chronic hypertension, prolonged high pressure shifts the autoregulatory range upward, making the kidneys reliant on high perfusion.  A sudden MAP drop (eg, from overtreatment) can cause AKI.  Diabetes mellitus promotes persistent afferent dilation (via multiple mechanisms), increasing glomerular hyperfiltration.  Over time, this damages the glomerular basement membrane, leading to proteinuria and nephropathy.  Both conditions impair perfusion stability, heightening AKI risk during hemodynamic stress. # Summary The kidneys maintain homeostasis through intricate filtration, reabsorption, and secretion mechanisms.  Cortical nephrons dominate solute reabsorption, whereas juxtamedullary nephrons establish the medullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication (allowing water reabsorption with concentration of urine). The glomerular filtration barrier combines size-selective (eg, glomerular basement membrane, podocytes) and charge-selective (ie, negatively charged glycoproteins) layers to exclude plasma proteins.  Tubular segments use specialized transporters to adjust filtrate composition, modulated by various hormones (eg, antidiuretic hormone, aldosterone). Renal hemodynamics are autoregulated via myogenic responses and tubuloglomerular feedback, maintaining the glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow across a wide range of mean arterial pressures (80-180 mm Hg).  Clinical biomarkers (eg, creatinine, cystatin C) and clearance techniques (eg, inulin clearance) quantify renal function.  Pharmacologic agents (eg, ACE inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors) target glomerular pressure to mitigate hyperfiltration injury.  Disrupted autoregulation (eg, NSAIDs, hypotension) precipitates acute kidney injury, underscoring the kidney's vulnerability to hemodynamic perturbations. ​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​

# Pulmonary Physiology: Respiratory Neurobiology # Introduction Respiratory neurobiology involves the structures and feedback mechanisms that determine breathing patterns and minute ventilation.  Respiratory control can be thought of as a central pattern generator (CPG) (brainstem) with both voluntary inputs (eg, cortical override) and involuntary inputs (eg, chemoreceptors). # Central pattern generator The respiratory CPG is a group of brainstem structures that work together to create a normal, unconscious (automatic) **tidal breathing pattern**.  The CPG consists of the medullary and pontine respiratory centers ((Figure 1)). ## Medullary respiratory center The medullary respiratory center sets the tidal **respiratory rate**.  It contains: - A **pacemaker** nucleus (the pre-Bötzinger complex):  This structure consists of thousands of neurons that spontaneously depolarize (eg, If sodium leak channel), establishing **automaticity**. - A **motor** nucleus (the ventral respiratory group \[VRG\]):  It receives rhythm input from the pacemaker and sends output to the **phrenic motor nucleus** (C3-5) to initiate diaphragm contraction and inspiratory effort; it also projects motor neurons to the accessory muscles of breathing. - A **sensory** nucleus (the dorsal respiratory group \[DRG\]):  It receives **afferent signals** from chemoreceptors (eg, pH, CO2, O2) and mechanoreceptors (eg, pulmonary stretch).  The DRG integrates these signals and accelerates or decelerates the pacemaker nucleus, subsequently quickening or slowing the respiratory rate. ## Pontine respiratory center The pontine respiratory center sets the **inspiratory time**.  It consists of the pneumotaxic and apneustic centers.  They have opposing effects on the VRG, which activates the diaphragm. - The **pneumotaxic center** shortens inspiration (tonic effect). - The **apneustic center** prolongs inspiration. The balance between them determines the transition between inspiration and expiration.  Under normal conditions, inspiration (I) lasts half as long as expiration (E) does (ie, I:E = 1:2) because the pneumotaxic center dominates.  Obstructive conditions are associated with longer expiration (eg, I:E = 1:3), whereas restrictive conditions are associated with longer inspiration (eg, I:E = 1:1). # Modulators of the central pattern generator The unconscious CPG can be modulated by voluntary control (eg, cortex), emotional responses (eg, limbic system), and feedback from chemoreceptors (pH, CO2, O2) and mechanoreceptors. ## Cortical and limbic input - Cortical input (voluntary):  Respiratory patterns can be controlled by the premotor and motor cortices (eg, speech, singing).  However, if pH drops or CO2 levels rise excessively (eg, prolonged breath holding), the medullary respiratory center overrides the cortex, triggering an involuntary breath. - Limbic input (involuntary):  Strong emotions (eg, fear, excitement) can cause involuntary changes in respiration via the **amygdala** and other limbic structures (cingulate cortex, hypothalamus) that project to the respiratory centers. ## Chemoreceptor input Chemoreceptors regulate respiration by detecting changes in pH, CO2, and O2 and adjusting breathing patterns accordingly ((Table 1)).  In order of importance: - **Arterial pH (H****+****)** and **CO****2**:  These are sensed by **peripheral** chemoreceptors (aortic arch, carotid bodies), which send afferents to the DRG via the vagus nerve (CN X) (aortic arch) and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) (carotid body) ((Figure 2)).  Low pH (acidosis) or high CO2 (hypercapnia) stimulates respiratory rate and depth. - **Low arterial pH** is a **more powerful** stimulus than CO2 and usually causes marked dyspnea.  For example, during diabetic ketoacidosis (eg, pH 7.28), patients continue to hyperventilate (eg, Kussmaul breathing) despite low PaCO2 (eg, 17 mm Hg).  In addition, unlike pH receptors, CO2 chemoreceptors become desensitized with chronic hypercapnia and renal compensation (eg, obesity hypoventilation syndrome). - **Central** chemoreceptors in the medulla sense CO2 **indirectly** by detecting changes in H+ concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).  When CO2 diffuses into the CSF, it creates H+ (ie, CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ **H****+** + HCO3) with the help of carbonic anhydrase. - **Arterial O****2**:  This is also sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies.  Low O2 (hypoxemia) stimulates respiratory rate and depth.  Compared to pH and CO2, hypoxemia is a weaker stimulus and generally does not cause significant dyspnea. ## Mechanoreceptor input Breathing patterns can be modulated by afferents from mechanoreceptors in the lungs. - **Pulmonary stretch receptors** are mechanosensitive ion channels located primarily in the airway wall, blood vessels, and pleural surfaces.  The key receptors, **Piezo1** and **Piezo2**, convert mechanical deformation into electrical signals (ie, piezoelectric effect).  When the lungs expand, these receptors send inhibitory signals to the medullary respiratory center, terminating inspiration to **prevent lung overinflation** (Hering-Breuer reflex). - **Alveolar juxtacapillary receptors (C fibers)** are chemosensitive and mechanosensitive sensory nerves located in the alveolar septa near pulmonary capillaries.  They respond to pulmonary congestion (eg, edema), inflammation, and noxious stimuli.  Activation triggers afferent signals via the vagus nerve to the medullary respiratory center, producing a **sensation of dyspnea** and reflex tachypnea. # Abnormal respiratory patterns ## "-pneas" Abnormal breath types are formally referred to by the suffix "-pnea": - Tachypnea refers to an abnormally rapid respiratory rate (eg, >20/min at rest). - Hyperpnea refers to an abnormally deep inspiratory volume. - Bradypnea refers to an abnormally slow respiratory rate (eg, <12/min at rest). - Hypopnea refers to an abnormally shallow inspiratory volume. - Apnea refers to a complete cessation of airflow. In practice, breathing patterns are often described by their gross appearance and tend to have classic associations.  For example, rapid deep breathing (ie, Kussmaul) is associated with metabolic acidosis; slow, shallow breathing is associated with respiratory depression (eg, opioid intoxication). ## Kussmaul Kussmaul respiration is a pattern of rapid, deep breathing associated with acute **metabolic acidosis** (eg, diabetic ketoacidosis, toxic alcohol ingestion).  It represents respiratory compensation through hyperventilation to induce respiratory alkalosis ((Video 1)). ## Cheyne-Stokes Cheyne-Stokes respiration is a periodic breathing pattern that **alternates** between hyperventilation (rapid, deep breathing) followed by hypopnea (shallow, slow breathing) or complete apnea.  The cycle repeats every 30 seconds to 2 minutes.  It is associated with: - Severe **heart failure**. - Stroke or diffuse brain injury. - Metabolic derangements (eg, uremia). Normally, rising arterial CO2 levels immediately signal the medulla to increase minute ventilation to quickly blow CO2 back down to normal ranges.  In Cheyne-Stokes respiration, **delayed feedback** from central chemoreceptors (eg, sluggish circulation in heart failure) causes CO2 to rise excessively.  This is followed by overcorrection via hyperventilation, causing CO2 levels to drop too low.  The low CO2 levels suppress the chemoreceptors, triggering hypoventilation or apnea until CO2 builds up again.  This restarts the cycle of apnea followed by gradually increasing and then decreasing (crescendo-decrescendo) tidal volumes  ((Video 2)). ## Ondine curse Ondine curse refers to central hypoventilation due to congenital (eg, *PHOX2B* mutation) or acquired lesions (eg, tumor) affecting the **medullary** respiratory center.  Automatic involuntary respiration is lost, particularly during sleep.  Sensitivity to acidosis or hypercapnia is also severely blunted or lost entirely.  Constant voluntary effort is required (ie, the patient must always remember to breathe).  It usually requires lifelong mechanical ventilation. ## Apneustic breathing Apneustic breathing is a pattern of prolonged inspiration, a long pause, and a very short expiration, which is associated with **pontine damage** (eg, herniation).  The pons regulates the inspiratory time through its pneumotaxic versus apneustic centers. ## Ataxic (Bitot) breathing Ataxic (Bitot) breathing involves erratic, unpredictable breaths that vary significantly in frequency, duration, and depth.  It is associated with **widespread damage** to multiple areas of the CPG (eg, pons, medulla). ## Agonal breathing Agonal breathing is a disorganized respiratory pattern that occurs in patients **near death**; it is characterized by irregular gasping or guppy-like breaths.  It results from generalized dysfunction of all respiratory control centers and is often accompanied by loss of upper airway tone (eg, gurgling, death-rattle). # Summary The brainstem's central pattern generator, consisting of medullary and pontine centers, establishes an automatic tidal pattern that can be modified by voluntary and involuntary inputs.  The medullary respiratory centers (pre-Bötzinger complex, dorsal and ventral respiratory groups) set the native respiratory rate, whereas the pontine centers (pneumotaxic and apneustic centers) determine inspiratory duration.  Tidal breathing can be modulated by voluntary control (eg, cortex), emotional responses (eg, limbic system), and feedback from chemoreceptors (pH, CO2, O2) and mechanoreceptors (eg, muscle spindles).  Abnormal patterns include Cheyne-Stokes respiration (eg, heart failure), Kussmaul respiration (eg, metabolic acidosis), and apneustic breathing (eg, pontine injury). ​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​
