articles.markdown: # Pulmonary Physiology: Respiratory Mechanics # Introduction Respiratory mechanics describe how pressure, volume, and flow are related to each other in the respiratory system.  This article integrates principles of physics and physiology to discuss the interaction between the lungs and chest wall, the process of normal tidal respiration, and the work of breathing. # Lungs and chest wall The respiratory system consists of the **lungs** and **chest wall**, which are considered **independent** elements because they are anatomically separated.  Changes in the lungs do not affect the intrinsic properties of the chest wall, and vice versa.  However, changes in either affect the entire respiratory system in an additive manner. ## Functional residual capacity The lungs and chest wall have opposing natural tendencies: - The lungs have a tendency to recoil inward (collapsing force) due to the elastin content of lung tissue. - The chest wall has a tendency to recoil outward (expanding force) due to the curvature of the ribs and intrinsic tension in the intercostal muscles. The lungs pull the chest wall inward, and the chest wall pulls the lungs outward.  The point where these forces balance each other is the **functional residual capacity (FRC)** ((Figure 1)).  FRC is the natural resting state of the respiratory system in the absence of voluntary effort.  It is equivalently described as the volume of air remaining in the lungs after normal passive exhalation. Tidal breathing begins from FRC because it minimizes energy expenditure.  Maintaining lung volumes above or below FRC requires additional muscular effort, which can be simulated—holding the breath above FRC requires effort to counter inward lung recoil, similar to keeping a spring stretched out.  Holding the breath below FRC requires effort to counter outward chest wall recoil, similar to compressing a spring.  Pathologic conditions can increase or decrease FRC.  FRC decreases when lung recoil increases (eg, interstitial fibrosis) or when chest wall recoil decreases (eg, pectus excavatum).  Conversely, FRC increases when lung recoil decreases (eg, emphysema) or when chest wall recoil increases (eg, pectus carinatum \[rare\]). ## Respiratory system compliance Compliance (C) describes how volume (V) changes in response to pressure (P) (ie, C = ΔV/ΔP).  Noncompliant (stiff) objects experience minimal change in volume when pressure is applied.  Normal respiratory system compliance (CRS) is 100 mL/cm H2O (each additional centimeter of water of pressure should inflate the lungs by 100 mL). Several disease states can alter CRS by affecting the lungs or chest wall: - Lung compliance (CL) decreases with interstitial stiffening (eg, pulmonary fibrosis) or alveolar filling processes (eg, pulmonary edema, pneumonia).  It increases with emphysema. - Chest wall compliance (CCW) decreases with thoracic cage deformities (eg, kyphosis), arthritis (eg, costochondral joints), extreme obesity, restrictive pleural disease (eg, adhesions, fibrothorax), or rare dystonic drug reactions (eg, serotonin syndrome).  It does not increase. The relationship between the 3 compliances is as follows:  1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW. ## Lung hysteresis In a pressure-volume diagram, CL is often shown as a relatively straight line with a slope of ΔV/ΔP ((Figure 2)).  This line represents inspiration only.  When both inspiration and expiration are graphed, the result is a loop—at a given pressure, the lungs hold more volume during expiration than inspiration ((Figure 3)).  This is called **hysteresis**. Hysteresis occurs because surfactant spreads out during inflation, reducing its concentration and requiring more pressure to overcome surface tension.  During expiration, surfactant concentration increases again.  The process of hysteresis is somewhat analogous to how memory foam slowly returns to its original shape after being compressed.  Loss of surfactant (eg, in acute respiratory distress syndrome) reduces hysteresis (resulting in a narrower loop) and lowers CL (resulting in a steeper slope). # Tidal breathing Tidal respiration refers to quiet breathing that occurs under normal conditions.  In adults, normal tidal volume is approximately 500 mL, corresponding to approximately 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight. ## Respiratory muscles - **Inspiration** is an active (effort-dependent) process requiring muscular effort.  The primary muscle of inspiration is the **diaphragm**.  In patients with dyspnea or respiratory distress, accessory muscles of inspiration can be activated; these include the neck strap muscles (eg, sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) and, in extreme cases, additional chest muscles (eg, pectoralis minor, trapezius, latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior). - In contrast, **expiration** is a passive (effort-independent) process that utilizes the natural recoil of the respiratory system.  No muscular effort is typically required.  However, in patients with dyspnea or respiratory distress, accessory muscles of expiration, including the internal **intercostals** and **abdominal wall** muscles (eg, obliques, transversus abdominus), may be used. Greater effort during inspiration shortens inspiratory time.  Conversely, greater effort during expiration does not shorten the expiratory time because the additional force produces dynamic airway collapse, delaying the expiratory airflow.  This can be observed by comparing the time required to exhale all the way to residual volume gently versus forcefully—despite the additional force, the time remains the same. ## Normal pressure swings There are 2 key pressures that govern breathing: the alveolar pressure and the pleural pressure.  These are measured in centimeters of H2O, with atmospheric pressure set to 0 cm H2O by convention. - **Alveolar pressure (Palveolar)**:  The pressure inside the lungs.  Air flows from areas of higher pressure to areas of lower pressure.  Inspiratory airflow occurs when Palveolar is negative (eg, −2 cm H2O), creating a gradient between the atmosphere (ie, mouth and nose) and the lungs; conversely, expiratory airflow occurs when Palveolar is positive (eg, 2 cm H2O) ((Figure 4)). - **Pleural (intrapleural) pressure (Ppleural)**:  The pressure in the pleural cavity (ie, between the lungs and chest wall).  Because the lungs and chest wall are constantly trying to pull apart from each other, Ppleural is always negative (eg, −5 cm H2O).  During inspiration, the diaphragm moves downward, and Ppleural becomes even more negative (eg, to -8 cm H2O), encouraging the lungs to expand. **Transpulmonary (transpleural) pressure (PTP)**:  The difference between alveolar (ie, inside the lungs) and pleural (ie, outside the lungs) pressure.  PTP is always slightly positive because Palveolar is always higher than Ppleural (even when both are negative).  The positive PTP keeps the lungs inflated against the chest wall throughout both inspiration and expiration. # Disrupted mechanics As discussed above, the transpulmonary pressure (PTP) is always slightly positive.  Normal PTP = Palveolar – Ppleural = (–2) – (–8) = 6 cm H2O.  Several situations can disrupt this relationship, resulting in PTP that is excessively positive, zero, or negative. ## High PTP An excessively high PTP occurs if Palveolar becomes too positive (↑↑ Palveolar) or Ppleural becomes too negative (↓↓ Ppleural): - **Palveolar can become too positive** during mechanical ventilation (with inappropriate settings), violent coughing, or severe air trapping (eg, asthma exacerbation). - **Ppleural can become too negative** with fibrotic lung disease, causing the lung to retract away from the chest wall.  It can also become too negative during forceful inhalation against a closed glottis (Müller maneuver), as seen in hanging injuries or severe obstructive sleep apnea. Dangerously elevated PTP (eg, >30 cm H2O) can cause barotrauma such as pleural rupture and pneumothorax, especially if there is underlying weakness of the lung tissue (eg, emphysematous bleb).  Excessive distention of the alveoli can also damage them, causing edema or hemorrhage. ## Zero PTP PTP falls to zero with a **spontaneous pneumothorax** (eg, ruptured bleb).  This occurs because Ppleural equalizes with atmospheric pressure through the lung defect.  Palveolar also remains at zero because the lung cannot retain volume as air escapes through the hole.  Loss of P**TP** causes the lung to collapse under its intrinsic elastic recoil. ## Negative PTP A negative P**TP** occurs when Ppleural exceeds Palveolar.  It occurs in 2 scenarios: - **Tension pneumothorax**:  During standard pneumothorax, Ppleural is zero (ie, atmospheric pressure).  However, in tension pneumothorax, Ppleural becomes positive if air continues to enter the pleural space faster than it can escape.  The high Ppleural compresses the lung and mediastinal structures.  This situation also develops with a sucking chest wound, a type of penetrating chest wall injury that creates a tissue flap allowing air to enter but not escape. - **Flail chest**:  Normally, the ribcage changes position in unison with the lungs, moving outward with inspiration and inward with expiration.  If a section of the chest wall breaks free (eg, ≥3 consecutive ribs are each fractured in ≥2 places), the ribcage paradoxically moves inward with inspiration.  This may cause the Ppleural to become positive with inspiration, limiting the ability of the lungs to fill. # Work of breathing ## Resistive and elastic The work of breathing (WOB) is composed of 2 components, resistive and elastic work. **Resistive work** is the energy required to overcome resistance to airflow.  It depends on: - **Airway resistance**:  Mainly determined by **airway diameter** (resistance ∝ 1/diameter4).  Airway resistance increases in conditions that narrow or obstruct the airway, such as asthmatic bronchospasm and mucus plugging.  Low lung volumes (eg, atelectasis) also increase airway resistance because the airway caliber is reduced. - **Respiratory rate**:  High respiratory rates produce faster airflow velocities, increasing turbulence, fiction against the bronchial tree, and air resistance. **Elastic work** is the energy required to overcome the intrinsic elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall.  Work is required to distend these structures even when flow is absent.  Elastic work depends on: - **Elastance**:  Respiratory system elastance is the inverse of **compliance** (ERS = 1/CRS).  It is elevated in conditions that decrease CL (eg, interstitial fibrosis, pulmonary edema) or CCW (eg, obesity, kyphosis). - **Tidal volume**:  Elastic work is increased with larger tidal volumes due to the additional recoil of the lung tissue and chest wall as they are stretched. ## Optimization of work of breathing Total WOB is the sum of the energy expenditure of the resistive and elastic components of the respiratory system ((Figure 5)). Humans unconsciously minimize the work required to maintain normal minute ventilation (VE), which is defined as the product of respiratory rate (RR) and tidal volume (VT) (VE = RR × VT).  As outlined above, resistive WOB increases with lower lung volume and higher respiratory rate; in contrast, elastic WOB increases with higher lung volume and lower respiratory rate.  Optimal WOB strikes a balance between these extremes, with RR of 12-14/min and VT of 400-600 mL.  This balance changes with obstructive or restrictive conditions: - In obstructive lung diseases (eg, asthma), resistive work is optimized by decreasing airway resistance (eg, bronchodilator therapy) and adopting a slower, deeper breathing pattern to minimize airflow turbulence. - In restrictive lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), elastic work is optimized by adopting a rapid, shallow breathing pattern, which trades greater resistive work (eg, faster airflow) for less elastic work (eg, lower tidal volume). Normally, not much work is required for tidal breathing (eg, 2%-5% of total basal energy expenditure).  As resistance or elastance increases, greater muscular effort is required to produce the same tidal volume.  For example, in advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), WOB can increase to as much as 30%-40% of total energy expenditure.  This chronically increased energy demand contributes to **pulmonary cachexia**.  WOB can dramatically increase during acute exacerbations, leading to respiratory failure if patients develop muscle fatigue. # Summary Respiratory mechanics describe how pressure, volume, and flow change during breathing.  The lungs and chest wall are components of the respiratory system with opposing tendencies: The lungs recoil inward due to elastin, whereas the chest wall recoils outward due to rib curvature.  These forces are balanced at functional residual capacity, the natural resting lung volume after passive exhalation.  Normal tidal breathing involves effort-dependent inspiration driven by the diaphragm and effort-independent expiration driven by natural recoil.  The work of breathing consists of resistive and elastic components.  Resistive work overcomes airflow resistance and is determined by airway resistance and respiratory rate; elastic work overcomes lung and chest wall recoil and is determined by respiratory system elastance (the inverse of compliance) and tidal volume. ​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​

articles.markdown: # Pulmonary Physiology: Pulmonary Circulation # Introduction The pulmonary circulation refers to blood flow from the right side of the heart, through the lungs, and to the left side of the heart.  Normal pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance, low-pressure system.  This article discusses the factors that influence pulmonary vascular resistance and the ways that the right ventricle (RV) responds to changes in its afterload. # Properties In anatomic order, the pulmonary circulation includes the RV, RV outflow tract, main pulmonary artery (PA), pulmonary arterial branches, pulmonary arterioles, pulmonary capillaries, pulmonary venules, pulmonary veins, and left atrium (LA). The pulmonary circulation handles the same cardiac output (CO) as the systemic circulation, in keeping with the continuity of flow principle (Qpulmonary = Qsystemic).  To accommodate this same flow within the lungs' smaller volume, the pulmonary circulation has **high compliance**.  Pulmonary arteries have thinner walls with less elastin and smooth muscle, allowing greater distensibility compared to systemic arteries.  Along with its high compliance, the pulmonary circulation is a **low-resistance, low-pressure** system: - Low resistance:  Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is approximately one-sixth of systemic vascular resistance (SVR):  PVR = 30-200 dynes·s/cm5, whereas SVR = 800-1200 dynes·s/cm5. - Low pressure:  Mean PA pressure (mPAP) is approximately one-sixth of mean arterial pressure (MAP):  mPAP = 15 mm Hg, whereas MAP = 90 mm Hg. # Right heart catheterization ## Procedure Right heart catheterization (ie, Swan-Ganz) records pressures at key points in the pulmonary circulation ((Figure 1)).  A catheter is introduced via the internal jugular or femoral veins and advanced into the superior vena cava.  Waveform and pressure readings are captured at the following: - Right atrium:  The classic central venous waveform (a, c, v, x, y) is seen ((Figure 2)).  The average value of all wave heights is the mean right atrial pressure. - RV:  When the catheter enters the RV, a sine waveform appears, ranging from 0-5 mm Hg at the end of diastole to approximately 25 mm Hg during peak systole. - PA:  As the catheter advances from the RV into the main PA, a pressure step-up occurs immediately after the catheter crosses the pulmonic valve.  Unlike the RV, the PA retains pressure during diastole due to vascular resistance and pulmonic valve closure.  This establishes a PA diastolic pressure (dPAP), which is approximately 10 mm Hg.  The PA systolic pressure (sPAP) closely matches the RV systolic pressure, which is approximately 25 mm Hg. - Wedge:  The catheter has a small balloon at its tip that allows it to lodge in a distal pulmonary artery ((Image 1)).  The pressure at this location is known as the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP).  When wedged, the catheter tip is isolated from the proximal PA pressure (due to the balloon) and detects only pressure transmitted backward from the pulmonary veins and LA.  Therefore, PCWP is a surrogate for LA pressure (LAP) ((Figure 3)).  Normally, PCWP is 5-8 mm Hg. Pressures collected during right heart catheterization are used to calculate PVR. ## Calculation of PVR From the Ohm law, the pressure drop across a circuit is equal to the flow multiplied by the resistance of the circuit (ΔP = Q × R).  In the pulmonary circulation: - ΔP is the difference between the main PA and LA.  Therefore, ΔP = mPAP − LAP. - mPAP = ⅓ × sPAP + ⅔ × dPAP = ⅓ × 25 + ⅔ × 10 = 15 mm Hg in healthy adults (because more time is spent in diastole than in systole).  As discussed previously, PAP is measured during right-sided heart catheterization of the main pulmonary artery. - LAP ≈ PCWP = 8 mm Hg in healthy adults.  As discussed previously, PCWP is measured during right-sided heart catheterization by occluding the distal pulmonary artery. - Q is the CO, or the total flow through the lungs.  CO is measured during right-sided heart catheterization using thermodilution (temperature curve after cold bolus injection into the PA) or the Fick method (difference in oxygen saturation between arterial and mixed venous blood).  Under normal conditions, CO ≈ 5 L/min. Therefore, substituting these values into ΔP = Q × R, the equation becomes (mPAP − LAP) = CO × PVR.  Rearranging this equation yields PVR = (mPAP − LAP) / CO ≈ (15 − 8)/5 = 1.4 mm Hg / (L/min) = 1.4 Wood units (wU).  (To convert between wU and dynes·s/cm5, the units of the International System of Units, multiply by 80.) ## Interpretation of PVR Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is defined as elevated mean PAP >20 mm Hg.  PH can occur with elevated or normal PVR: - **PH with elevated PVR** (≥3 wU):  In this scenario, PH is due to remodeling of the PAs and arterioles (the resistance vessels).  Known as **precapillary PH**, this encompasses PA hypertension (PAH, Group 1), PH due to chronic lung disease or hypoxemia (Group 3), and PH due to chronic pulmonary thromboembolism (Group 4). - **PH with normal PVR** (<3 wU):  In this scenario, PH is due to the transmission of venous pressure backward from the left atrium.  Known as **postcapillary PH**, this encompasses PH due to left-sided heart disease (eg, heart failure) or mitral valve disease (Group 2).  This is the most common cause of PH in the United States.  PCWP is expected to be elevated (eg, >15 mm Hg). # Determinants of PVR PVR is determined by vascular tone, compression, recruitment, and remodeling. ## Vascular tone The balance between endogenous vasoconstrictors and vasodilators sets the vascular tone. - The major pulmonary **vasodilators** include nitric oxide and prostacyclin (or prostaglandin I2). - The major pulmonary **vasoconstrictors** include endothelin-1 and catecholamines (eg, epinephrine).  Pulmonary vasoconstriction is also stimulated by hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis, as well as by other vascular mediators such as angiotensin II, serotonin, and leukotrienes. ## Vascular compression Pulmonary capillaries are divided into extraalveolar (interstitial) and intraalveolar vessels. - At low lung volumes (near residual volume), extraalveolar vessels are compressed, but intraalveolar vessels remain open. - Conversely, at high lung volumes (near total lung capacity), extraalveolar vessels are open, whereas intraalveolar vessels are compressed. Both vessel types are maximally open at intermediate lung volumes (near functional residual capacity) ((Figure 4)). Like alveolar volume, alveolar pressure has a direct effect on vascular compression.  High positive airway pressure (eg, mechanical ventilation) can compress all capillaries, raising PVR. ## Vascular recruitment At rest, only around 66% of the pulmonary vessels are open.  The remaining 33%, particularly at the lung apices, are unperfused.  During exertion, increased CO recruits these underperfused vessels while the other vessels distend to accommodate the higher blood volume.  This combination of **recruitment and distension** helps keep PVR stable despite increased blood flow. ## Vascular remodeling Normal PA have a relatively thin wall.  In PH, the arteries can undergo structural changes, including neointimal hyperplasia, smooth muscle thickening, and adventitial fibrosis ((Figure 5)).  The vascular bed can be obliterated by emphysema or obstructed by chronic thromboemboli. Remodeled vessels progressively lose their ability to respond to vasodilators and vasoconstrictors.  In advanced stages, they may become completely unresponsive.  These structural changes are typically irreversible and contribute to elevated PVR. # RV function ## RV versus LV The RV has several key functional differences from the LV: - **Preload tolerance**:  The RV adapts well to sudden increases in preload due to its high compliance; in contrast, the LV adapts poorly due to its low compliance (eg, volume overload can quickly lead to pulmonary congestion and edema). - **Afterload tolerance**:  The LV adapts well to sudden increases in afterload, whereas the RV adapts poorly (eg, a sudden increase in PA pressure, such as acute pulmonary embolism, can quickly lead to RV dilation and failure). - **Contraction**:  RV myocytes are arrayed linearly, so the ventricle contracts lengthwise, and RV ejection fraction is best assessed by **longitudinal shortening**.  In contrast, LV myocytes are arrayed helically, so the ventricle contracts torsionally, and LV ejection fraction is best assessed by circumferential contraction. - **Ventricular interdependence**:  The LV "owns" the septum, whereas the RV "borrows" the septum for contractile efficiency.  RV pressure overload (eg, severe PH) or pericardial constriction (eg, tuberculosis) leads to septal bowing into the LV, compromising its filling and subsequent output (eg, pulsus paradoxus).  Conversely, LV pressure overload does not move the septum to the right and has minimal impact on RV filling. - **Coronary perfusion**:  The LV is perfused only during diastole when intraventricular pressure drops below coronary artery pressure.  In contrast, the RV, with its lower pressure, is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle ((Figure 6)).  Therefore, the RV is more vulnerable to hypotension and ischemia due to its reliance on continuous perfusion. ## RV-PA coupling As discussed, the RV is much more **afterload sensitive** than the LV.  If too sudden, even a small increase in PAP (eg, 20 mm Hg) can cause acute RV dysfunction.  This explains why signs of RV dysfunction (eg, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension) typically appear earlier than signs of low CO (eg, hypotension, cool extremities). Over long periods, the RV hypertrophies to adapt to high afterload.  This maintains **ventriculoarterial (RV-PA) coupling** despite the high PAP.  Patients with chronic PH can often have PAP approaching or even exceeding systemic pressures but appear remarkably well compensated due to RV adaptation.  However, some conditions can induce concurrent myocardial fibrosis (eg, scleroderma, sarcoidosis), impairing RV coupling and leading to earlier failure and more significant symptoms at comparatively lower PAP.  RV coupling is also impaired by factors that depress myocardial contractility (eg, cytokines, ischemia, acidosis, beta blockers).  Coupling can be conceptualized as the ratio of RV contractility to RV afterload. # Summary The pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance, low-pressure, and high-compliance system that transports blood from the right side of the heart, through the lungs, and to the left side of the heart.  Pulmonary vascular resistance is influenced by vascular tone (eg, nitric oxide, endothelin-1), physical compression (eg, high lung volume), vessel recruitment (eg, exercise), and structural remodeling (eg, medial thickening).  The right ventricle is highly sensitive to afterload and can acutely fail, with sudden increases in pulmonary artery pressure. ​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​

# Pulmonary Physiology: Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve # Introduction Oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) must be transported efficiently between the lungs and tissues through the bloodstream.  Most O2 is transported via the carrier protein hemoglobin, whereas most CO2 is transported in the form of bicarbonate (HCO3−).  Hemoglobin has unique properties that create varying affinity for O2 and help optimize O2 loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues.  These are reflected in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.  Several factors influence the overall affinity of hemoglobin for O2, allowing the body to adjust O2 loading and unloading as needed. # Gas transport and the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve ## Hemoglobin structure and cooperative binding Hemoglobin is a tetrameric hemeprotein contained within red blood cells (RBCs).  It is usually composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains, each containing a heme group capable of binding a single O2 molecule; therefore, each hemoglobin molecule can bind up to 4 O2 molecules ((Figure 1)).  Most O2 in the blood (~98%) is carried by hemoglobin, whereas a small percentage is transported dissolved in the plasma. The **oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve** illustrates the relationship between the degree of O2 saturation of hemoglobin and the partial pressure of O2 (PO2) dissolved in the blood.  The curve reflects hemoglobin's varying binding affinity for O2 and its ability to load O2 in the lungs and release O2 in the tissues. O2 binding to hemoglobin is cooperative, meaning that after a single O2 molecule binds, the conformation of hemoglobin changes and the remaining heme groups bind O2 more readily.  This **cooperative binding** interaction between hemoglobin subunits creates a characteristic sigmoidal (S-shaped) hemoglobin dissociation curve ((Figure 2)): - At very low PO2, hemoglobin is largely deoxygenated and its O2 affinity is relatively low, so the first O2 molecule binds poorly, and the curve is flat. - Once the first O2 molecule binds to 1 hemoglobin binding site, increased affinity of the remaining sites creates the steep middle portion of the curve. - With increasing PO2, more binding sites become occupied and hemoglobin approaches full saturation, creating the plateau portion of the curve. ## O2 loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues The cooperative nature of O2 binding allows hemoglobin to transport O2 efficiently between the lungs and the tissues. In the lungs, alveolar PO2 is typically around 100 mm Hg.  At this high O2 tension, hemoglobin operates on the plateau portion of the dissociation curve and becomes nearly fully saturated.  Because the plateau is relatively flat, moderate reductions in alveolar PO2 lead to only small reductions in hemoglobin saturation.  This acts as a safety mechanism because it helps maintain adequate O2 loading even when some degree of lung hypoxia is present. In the peripheral tissues, PO2 is typically around 40 mm Hg, which corresponds to the steep portion of the curve.  In this region, small reductions in PO2 create relatively large decreases in hemoglobin saturation.  This facilitates O2 release into the tissues. ## CO2 transport and the Bohr and Haldane effects The majority of CO2 is carried in the blood as HCO3− (~70%), whereas some is bound to hemoglobin and an additional small portion is transported dissolved in the plasma ((Figure 3)).  Molecular interactions, namely the Bohr and Haldane effects, contribute to the efficient transfer of O2 and CO2 in the lungs and tissues ((Figure 4)): - In the capillaries of the **peripheral tissues**, high levels of CO2 increase local (ambient) acidity, which decreases overall hemoglobin affinity for O2 (ie, shifts the entire oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right) and facilitates the unloading of O2 (factors that shift the entire dissociation curve are discussed later).  This is known as the **Bohr effect**.  CO2 combines with water (H2O), resulting in a hydrogen (H+) ion and HCO3−.  The H+ ions are carried by hemoglobin, whereas the HCO3− is transferred to the plasma for transport to the lungs. - In the capillaries of the **lungs**, binding of O2 molecules to hemoglobin decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for CO2, which facilitates the unloading of CO2 from hemoglobin.  The binding of O2 also increases the acidity of the hemoglobin molecule and facilitates the release of H+ ions from hemoglobin binding sites.  This is known as the **Haldane effect**.  The H+ ions combine with HCO3− to produce H2O and CO2.  The CO2 then crosses the alveolar capillary-membrane into the lungs and is expired. ## Role of bisphosphoglycerate RBCs do not have mitochondria and therefore use glycolysis, rather than oxidative phosphorylation, as the major pathway to generate energy.  During normal glycolysis, ATP is generated when 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) is converted to 3-phosphoglycerate by the enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase ((Figure 5)).  However, RBCs can bypass this part of the pathway using an enzyme called BPG mutase to convert 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG.  2,3-BPG binds to deoxyhemoglobin in a pocket between the 2 beta globin chains.  Positively charged amino acids within this pocket interact with the negatively charged phosphate groups of 2,3-BPG, allosterically reducing hemoglobin's affinity for O2.  The conversion of 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG is increased with hypoxemia or other conditions of low blood O2 content (eg, anemia):  Higher 2,3-BPG levels within RBCs facilitate easier delivery of O2 to the peripheral tissues. # Physiologic factors that shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve A commonly used parameter from the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is the P50, which is the PO2 at which 50% of hemoglobin binding sites are occupied by O2 molecules.  The average P50 of hemoglobin under normal conditions is 26 mm Hg, such that >50% of hemoglobin sites are occupied even in venous blood, where PO2 is generally approximately 40 mm Hg. Changes in the P50 reflect changes in the overall O2 affinity of hemoglobin: - **Lower P****50** indicates **higher O****2** **affinity** and manifests as a **left shift** of the entire curve. - **Higher P****50** indicates **lower O****2** **affinity** and manifests as a **right shift** of the entire curve. Several physiologic variables alter the O2 affinity of hemoglobin and shift the position of the dissociation curve ((Figure 6)): ## Rightward shift - A **rightward shift** indicates **decreased O****2** **affinity** and **encourages O****2** **release into the tissues**.  It also somewhat discourages O2 uptake in the lungs, but this effect is minimal because it involves the plateau portion of the dissociation curve.  A rightward shift is driven by conditions that increase O2 need in the tissues (eg, exercising muscle, elevated metabolic rate) and occurs with: - Decreased pH. - Increased temperature. - Increased 2,3-BPG. ## Leftward shift A **leftward shift** indicates **increased O****2** **affinity** and **discourages O****2** **release to the tissues**.  It also somewhat encourages O2 uptake in the lungs, but again, this effect is minimal at the plateau portion of the dissociation curve.  A leftward shift occurs with: - Increased pH. - Decreased temperature. - Decreased 2,3-BPG. # Hemoglobin A and other types of hemoglobin (different chain compositions) Hemoglobin, composed of 2 alpha chains and 2 beta chains, is the normal and most common type of adult hemoglobin.  It is referred to as **hemoglobin A**. ## Abnormal variants of hemoglobin A Genetic mutations (usually point mutations affecting a single amino acid) can create abnormal variants of hemoglobin A that have altered conformation and different O2 affinity than normal hemoglobin A. Increased O2 affinity variants include hemoglobin Chesapeake and hemoglobin Kempsey.  The increased affinity reduces O2 unloading in the tissues, creating tissue hypoxia that stimulates erythropoietin production and erythrocytosis (high RBC count). Decreased O2 affinity variants include hemoglobin C and hemoglobin sickle cell (hemoglobin S): - Hemoglobin C results in a decreased RBC lifespan and usually mild anemia.  Increased O2 unloading in the tissues allows most affected patients to generally remain asymptomatic. - Hemoglobin S allows increased O2 unloading in the tissues, but it creates other substantial disruptions.  Low PO2 encourages polymerization of hemoglobin S, which disrupts RBC shape and can impair blood flow.  RBC lifespan is markedly shortened, which can result in severe anemia. ## Other types of hemoglobin Other types of hemoglobin result from combinations of different types of globin chains ((Table 1)).  Relevant for O2 transport are the following: - **Fetal hemoglobin**:  Fetal hemoglobin (hemoglobin F) is synthesized primarily during fetal development (~8 weeks gestation until term) and consists of 2 alpha chains but with 2 gamma chains instead of beta chains.  The gamma chains do not bind effectively to 2,3-BPG due to the replacement of a histidine residue with serine ((Figure 7)); therefore, fetal hemoglobin has significantly higher O2 affinity than adult hemoglobin ((Figure 8)).  This allows fetal hemoglobin to extract more O2 from the adult hemoglobin in the placenta, providing the developing fetus with an adequate supply of O2. - **Hemoglobin H**:  Hemoglobin H is an abnormal hemoglobin composed of 4 beta chains.  It is dysfunctional and cannot effectively transport O2.  It is seen in adults with alpha thalassemia intermedia (substantially impaired production of alpha chains) ((Table 2)). - **Hemoglobin Bart**:  Hemoglobin Bart is an abnormal hemoglobin composed of 4 gamma chains.  It is dysfunctional and cannot effectively transport O2.  It is seen in fetuses with alpha thalassemia major (absent production of alpha chains), which is incompatible with life and usually results in intrauterine demise. # Other clinically important structural relatives of hemoglobin ## Carboxyhemoglobin Carbon monoxide (CO) has extremely high binding affinity for hemoglobin and is highly toxic (and potentially fatal) in anything other than small quantities.  CO outcompetes O2 for hemoglobin binding sites, and, once bound, creates carboxyhemoglobin, which has a dissociation curve shifted far to the left with an asymptotic (rather than sigmoid) shape ((Figure 9)).  Toxicity results from fewer O2 molecules being able to bind to hemoglobin, and those that do bind cannot be released into the tissues.  Carboxyhemoglobin is normally present in small amounts (eg, <1%-2% of all hemoglobin) but is present in higher quantities in smokers (eg, ~10%).  Higher blood levels, typically due to exposure to high levels of ambient CO (eg, house fire, faulty indoor heating equipment), are considered toxic. ## Myoglobin In contrast to hemoglobin, myoglobin is a monomeric heme protein and is the primary O2\-storage protein in skeletal and cardiac muscle.  Myoglobin has only 1 heme group and does not exhibit cooperative binding interactions; therefore, its O2\-dissociation curve has a hyperbolic shape ((Figure 10)).  The affinity of myoglobin for O2 is far higher than that of hemoglobin, with myoglobin having a P50 of only 1 mm Hg (compared to ~26 mm Hg for hemoglobin), such that myoglobin is highly saturated with O2 even in a low-O2 environment. # Summary Most oxygen is transported in the bloodstream via the carrier protein hemoglobin, whereas most carbon dioxide is transported in the form of bicarbonate (but some is carried by hemoglobin).  The most common type of normal adult hemoglobin (hemoglobin A) is composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains, and the unique structure allows for cooperative binding properties that help optimize oxygen loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues.  Factors that decrease the overall affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen (ie, shift the dissociation curve to the right) and facilitate oxygen delivery to the tissues include decreased pH, increased temperature, and increased 2,3- bisphosphoglycerate levels. ​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌

# Pulmonary Physiology: Hypoxemia

# Introduction

Hypoxemia, hypoxia, anemia, and ischemia are related, yet distinct processes:

-   **Hypoxemia**:  Low dissolved oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) content of arterial blood, commonly defined as an arterial partial pressure of O<sub>2</sub> (PaO<sub>2</sub>) <60 mm Hg.  Example:  parenchymal lung disease.
-   **Hypoxia**:  Low O<sub>2</sub> content at the end-organ and tissue level.  It can be caused by hypoxemia, anemia, or ischemia.  Prolonged hypoxia typically results in tissue necrosis.  Example:  myocardial infarction.
-   **Anemia**:  Low number of circulating red blood cells (and therefore, hemoglobin content) in arterial blood.  Example:  iron deficiency.
-   **Ischemia**:  Low perfusion of end-organs and tissues, resulting in decreased O<sub>2</sub> and other nutrients (eg, glucose).  Example:  arterial thrombosis.

This article discusses the mechanisms, pathophysiology, and evaluation of hypoxemia.

# Normal oxygenation

Normal oxygenation requires 3 elements:

-   Normal inspired O<sub>2</sub> (ie, normal PiO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Normal alveolar ventilation (ie, normal PaCO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (ie, normal A-a gradient).

## Normal inspired oxygen (PiO<sub>2</sub>)

**PiO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of inspired O<sub>2</sub>) is the O<sub>2</sub> available in the atmosphere for breathing.  It is determined by the fraction of inspired O<sub>2</sub> (FiO<sub>2</sub>), the atmospheric pressure (P<sub>atm</sub>), and the water vapor pressure (P<sub>H2O</sub>).

Under standard conditions:  PiO<sub>2</sub> = FiO<sub>2</sub> × (P<sub>atm</sub> − P<sub>H2O</sub>) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ **150 mm Hg**:

-   **FiO**<sub>**2**</sub> = fraction of inspired O<sub>2</sub>.  It is the percentage of air molecules that are O<sub>2</sub>.  Normal FiO<sub>2</sub> is 21% everywhere on Earth.
-   **P**<sub>**atm**</sub> = atmospheric pressure.  Normal P<sub>atm</sub> is 760 mm Hg at sea level and decreases with altitude.
-   **P**<sub>**H2O**</sub> = vapor pressure of water in the atmosphere.  Normal P<sub>H2O</sub> is 47 mm Hg.

## Normal alveolar ventilation (PaCO<sub>2</sub>)

**PaCO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide) reflects the effectiveness of ventilation, which removes ("blows off") carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>).  It is determined by minute ventilation, the product of respiratory rate (RR) and tidal volume (V<sub>T</sub>).  Normal minute ventilation is 6-8 L/min because normal RR is 12-16/min and normal V<sub>T</sub> is 500 mL (= 0.5 L).

PaCO<sub>2</sub> is measured directly by arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis.  PaCO<sub>2</sub> is in equilibrium with PACO<sub>2</sub> (partial pressure of alveolar carbon dioxide) because CO<sub>2</sub> diffuses instantly between the pulmonary capillary blood and the alveolar airspace.  Therefore, under normal conditions, P<sub>A</sub>CO<sub>2</sub> = PaCO<sub>2</sub> = **40 mm Hg**.

In the alveolus, each molecule of CO<sub>2</sub> displaces 0.8 molecule of O<sub>2</sub>.  **PAO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of alveolar oxygen) is the O<sub>2</sub> content present in the alveolar airspace after dilution by CO<sub>2</sub>.  Normally, P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = PiO<sub>2</sub> − P<sub>A</sub>CO<sub>2</sub> / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = **100 mm Hg**.

## Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (A-a gradient)

**A-a gradient** (alveolar-arterial gradient) is the difference between P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and PaO<sub>2</sub>.

-   P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is normally 100 mm Hg as previously described.
-   **PaO**<sub>**2**</sub> is normally **75-100 mm Hg** and is measured directly by ABG analysis.

A small A-a gradient is normally present due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, thebesian veins, bronchial circulation).  This expected A-a gradient can be predicted from age:  normal A-a gradient ≈ age / 3 ≈ (age / 4) + 4.  The A-a gradient is widened by conditions that disrupt the uptake of oxygen, such as V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, and abnormal right-to-left shunting.

# Five mechanisms of hypoxemia

There are 5 mechanisms of hypoxemia:

-   1\. Low PiO<sub>2</sub>.
-   2\. Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Abnormal (↑) A-a gradient.
    -   3\. V/Q mismatch.
    -   4\. Diffusion limitation.
    -   5\. Right-to-left shunt.

## Low inspired oxygen (↓P<sub>i</sub>O<sub>2</sub>)

Low PiO<sub>2</sub> refers to hypoxemia due to insufficient atmospheric O<sub>2</sub> available for breathing.  It occurs in 2 situations:

-   **Decreased FiO**<sub>**2**</sub> (ie, **normobaric hypoxemia**):  Normal FiO<sub>2</sub> is 21% everywhere on Earth.  It drops if another gas displaces O<sub>2</sub> in the inspired air.  For example, a massive nitrogen spill can severely depress FiO<sub>2</sub>, even though P<sub>atm</sub> remains the same.  In practice, this is a very rare scenario.
-   **Decreased P**<sub>**atm**</sub> (ie, **hypobaric hypoxemia**):  Normal P<sub>atm</sub> is 760 mm Hg at sea level.  Atmospheric pressure is decreased at **high altitudes**.  For example, P<sub>atm</sub> is only 250 mm Hg at the top of Mount Everest, even though FiO<sub>2</sub> is still 21%.  PaO<sub>2</sub> declines with rising elevation ((Figure 1)), with hypoxemia generally becoming problematic at >2,500 m (8,000 ft), corresponding to the development of high-altitude illness.

With low PiO<sub>2</sub>, hypoxemia occurs because the initial O<sub>2</sub> content reaching the alveoli is decreased.  However, the **A-a gradient is norma**l because O<sub>2</sub> transport across the alveolar membrane is unaffected.

## Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO<sub>2</sub>)

Alveolar hypoventilation ((Figure 2)) refers to hypoxemia due to the retention of carbon dioxide.  An increase in PaCO<sub>2</sub> **(hypercapnia)** occurs in 3 situations:

-   **Central hypoventilation** ("won't breathe"):  Central hypoventilation occurs when neural respiratory drive is diminished.  Etiologies include opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines, and damage to brainstem respiratory centers (eg, tumor, stroke).  Patients have **slow and shallow** breathing (↓ RR × ↓ V<sub>T</sub>), indicating a lack of drive.
-   **Peripheral hypoventilation** ("can't breathe"):  Peripheral hypoventilation occurs when respiratory mechanics are impaired, even though neural respiratory drive is intact.  Etiologies include neuromuscular disease (eg, myasthenia gravis), chest wall deformities (eg, severe kyphosis), advanced obstructive lung disease (eg, emphysema), and advanced restrictive lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis).  Patients have **rapid and shallow** breathing (↑ RR × ↓↓ V<sub>T</sub>), and minute ventilation decreases when tachypnea cannot compensate for low V<sub>T</sub>.
-   **High dead space** (wasted ventilation):  Dead space refers to the portion of the V<sub>T</sub> that does not participate in gas exchange.
    -   **Anatomic** dead space is formed where no gas exchange occurs in the conducting airways (eg, trachea, bronchi).  It remains constant but can be increased if additional tubing is added to the respiratory circuit (eg, mechanical ventilation).
    -   **Alveolar** dead space is formed by alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused.  It is normally negligible but can be increased by conditions that block alveolar perfusion (eg, pulmonary embolism).  Minute ventilation is decreased **despite** rapid and deep breathing (↑ RR × ↑ V<sub>T</sub>) because most of the V<sub>T</sub> does not participate in gas exchange.

With alveolar hypoventilation, hypoxemia occurs because O<sub>2</sub> is displaced by CO<sub>2</sub> retained in the alveoli.  However, **A-a gradient is normal** because O<sub>2</sub> transport across the alveolar membrane is intact.

## V/Q mismatch

V/Q mismatch ((Figure 3)) refers to hypoxemia due to a regional imbalance of air flow (V) and blood flow (Q) reaching the alveoli.  Normally, both V and Q are highest at lung bases and lowest at the lung apices.  Across the entire lung, this averages to a global V/Q ratio = 1 ((Figure 4)).  Defects in either V or Q can cause deviations from this ratio:

-   **Low V/Q** ((Figure 5)):  Alveoli are poorly ventilated but continue to be perfused.  Etiologies include **airway and airspace disorders** such as lobar pneumonia, asthmatic bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, and atelectasis.
-   **High V/Q** ((Figure 6)):  Alveoli are poorly perfused but continue to be ventilated.  Etiologies include **pulmonary vascular disorders** such as segmental pulmonary embolus and pulmonary arterial hypertension.  (These high V/Q areas also contribute to increased alveolar dead space, as previously described.)

With V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia occurs because Q and V are not efficiently localized together, producing an **elevated A-a gradient**.

## Diffusion limitation

Diffusion limitation ((figure 7)) refers to hypoxemia due to factors that impair O<sub>2</sub> transfer across the alveolar membrane.  Normally, O<sub>2</sub> diffuses quickly and is fully extracted by the time blood has traveled only a third of the pulmonary capillary length.  This explains why exercise, which can increase pulmonary Q, does not result in hypoxemia.  However, 2 major processes can limit diffusion:

-   **Destruction** of the alveolar membrane (eg, emphysema) decreases the surface area available for O<sub>2</sub> uptake.
-   **Thickening** of the alveolar membrane (eg, interstitial lung disease) increases the diffusion distance for O<sub>2</sub>.

Unlike V/Q mismatch, which involves regional or focal abnormalities (eg, segmental pulmonary embolus), diffusion limitation involves diffuse abnormalities of the lung parenchyma.

With diffusion limitation, hypoxemia occurs because O<sub>2</sub> transit across the alveolar membrane is impaired (ie, **elevated A-a gradient**).  In many cases, patients can be normoxic at rest but develop hypoxemia with exertion.

## Right-to-left shunting

Right-to-left shunting refers to hypoxemia due to the direct mixture of deoxygenated blood with oxygenated blood.  It occurs in 3 scenarios:

-   **Intracardiac anatomic shunt**:  An intracardiac communication is seen with atrial or ventricular septal defects.  Normally, oxygenated blood flows from the left chambers (higher pressure) to the deoxygenated right chambers (lower pressure).  However, the flow can reverse if the right-sided pressures increase, such as with the development of pulmonary hypertension, known as Eisenmenger syndrome ((Figure 8)).
-   **Intrapulmonary anatomic shunt**:  An intrapulmonary anatomic shunt is seen with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, which are anomalous connections between the deoxygenated pulmonary arteries and oxygenated pulmonary veins (bypassing the alveolar capillaries).
-   **Intrapulmonary shunt effect**:  In patients with extensive alveolar edema (eg, severe acute respiratory distress syndrome), the V/Q ratio can be close to 0, such that blood passing through the lungs barely receives oxygen.  This produces a functional right-to-left shunt, even though no direct anatomic connection is present.

With right-to-left shunting, hypoxemia occurs because deoxygenated blood mixes directly with oxygenated blood.  The **A-a gradient is elevated**.  Hypoxemia is often severe and **does not correct** with supplemental O<sub>2</sub> because a portion of the blood flow never reaches the lungs to be oxygenated.

# Evaluation of hypoxemia

ABG analysis can be approached in 2 ways.  A physiologic method, emphasizing stepwise interpretation without clinical context, is presented here.  In contrast, a clinical method, in which ABG is reserved for complex cases of hypoxemia in which clinical data alone are insufficient, is discussed in a separate article.  When reviewing an ABG, it is a good habit to apply a systematic framework even when the condition seems clinically obvious.

Formal stepwise ABG analysis of hypoxia ((Figure 9)) involves the 3 steps illustrated below.

## Step 1:  Compare PaO<sub>2</sub> and SaO<sub>2</sub>

PaO<sub>2</sub> is measured on ABG, and SaO<sub>2</sub> (O<sub>2</sub> saturation) is measured by pulse oximetry.  They are related by the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve ((Figure 10)); a left shift of the curve indicates increased hemoglobin O2 affinity and can be caused by increased pH, decreased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, and decreased temperature.  The PaO<sub>2</sub> at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated (P50) is a value used as a conventional measure of hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.

Dyshemoglobinemias can lead to discrepancies between PaO<sub>2</sub> and SaO<sub>2</sub>.

-   **Methemoglobinemia**:  Methemoglobin is hemoglobin in which iron is oxidized to the ferric (Fe<sup>3+</sup>) state, which cannot bind oxygen.  Therefore, the amount of functional hemoglobin available is reduced, leading to decreased SaO₂.  However, the amount of O<sub>2</sub> dissolved in plasma is normal (ie, arterial blood is normoxic), meaning that PaO<sub>2</sub> is normal.
-   **Carboxyhemoglobinemia**:  Carboxyhemoglobin forms when carbon monoxide (rather than oxygen) binds to hemoglobin.  Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light at a similar wavelength to oxyhemoglobin, causing pulse oximeters to misclassify it.  Therefore, SaO<sub>2</sub> (measured by pulse oximetry) reads as normal (or even artificially high), and blood may appear deceptively pink, even though functional oxygen-carrying capacity is reduced and true hypoxemia (eg, PaO<sub>2</sub> <60 mm Hg) may be present.

Additional testing for abnormal hemoglobin species (eg, multiwavelength CO-oximetry) may be indicated to explain the PaO<sub>2</sub>\-SaO<sub>2</sub> gap.

Severe acidosis or alkalosis can shift the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right or left, respectively.  For example, acidosis leads to the SaO<sub>2</sub> reading higher than expected for PaO<sub>2</sub> because it favors unloading into tissues.

## Step 2:  Calculate A-a gradient

The A-a gradient is a 4-step process that follows inspired gas as it moves from the atmosphere into the alveolar capillaries.

-   First, **calculate PiO**<sub>**2**</sub>:
    -   When breathing room air at sea level, PiO<sub>2</sub> = FiO<sub>2</sub> × (P<sub>atm</sub> − P<sub>H2O</sub>) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150 mm Hg.  This value changes at different altitudes or with the use of supplemental oxygen.
-   Second, **calculate P**<sub>**A**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub>:
    -   As discussed previously, P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is the alveolar O<sub>2</sub> content after dilution by CO<sub>2</sub>.  Each molecule of CO<sub>2</sub> displaces 0.8 molecules of O<sub>2</sub>.  PaCO<sub>2</sub> is taken from the ABG and is normally 40 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal PAO<sub>2</sub> = PiO<sub>2</sub> × PaCO<sub>2</sub> / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = 100 mm Hg.
-   Third, **calculate A-a gradient**:
    -   A-a gradient is the difference between P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (calculated above) and PaO<sub>2</sub> (measured from ABG).  For example, a normal PaO<sub>2</sub> = 90 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal A-a gradient = 100 − 90 = 10 mm Hg.
-   Finally, **determine expected A-a gradient for age**:
    -   The physiologic A-a gradient increases with age.  Expected A-a gradient = (age / 4) + 4 ≈ age / 3.  The calculated A-a gradient in the previous step should be compared to this expected value.  A normal A-a gradient is due to low PiO<sub>2</sub> or alveolar hypoventilation.  An elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunt.

An example using real patient data is provided in the table ((Table 1)).

## Step 3a:  If A-a gradient is normal

Hypoxemia with normal A-a gradient is due to alveolar hypoventilation (most common) or low PiO<sub>2</sub> (usually clinically obvious).

-   **Alveolar hypoventilation** is indicated by elevated PaCO<sub>2</sub> (ie, >45 mm Hg).
-   **Low PiO**<sub>**2**</sub>, such as high altitude, is usually accompanied by low PaCO<sub>2</sub> due to hyperventilation.

## Step 3b:  If A-a gradient is elevated

Hypoxemia with elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  These can be differentiated by the response to supplemental oxygen.

-   **V/Q mismatch** or **diffusion limitation**:  The hypoxemia responds quickly to supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide but remains relatively constant at all levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    -   On room air:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 100 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    -   On 40% FiO<sub>2</sub>:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 240 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 190, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg still.  (The higher starting PiO<sub>2</sub> can "overcome" the A-a gradient to normalize the PaO<sub>2</sub>.)
-   **Right-to-left shunting**:  Hypoxemia does not respond to any level of supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide and continues to increase at higher levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    -   On room air:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 100 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    -   On 100% FiO<sub>2</sub>:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 660 but PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50 still.  (Even pure O<sub>2</sub> is ineffective because shunted blood bypasses the alveoli entirely.)

# Effects of hypoxemia

## Tissue responses

Tissue hypoxia is sensed by hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF1ɑ) (Figure 11)).  HIF1ɑ is a transcription factor that is constitutively expressed by most cells.  In normoxic cytosol, HIF1ɑ is constantly degraded; in contrast, in hypoxic cytosol, it is posttranslationally stabilized.  HIF1ɑ can have adaptive or potentially maladaptive effects, depending on the severity and duration of hypoxia:

-   **Erythropoiesis**:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of erythropoietin in kidney juxtaglomerular cells and stimulates iron uptake in gut epithelium ((Figure 12)).
    -   Adaptively, this allows for compensatory polycythemia (generally, hematocrit >50% and hemoglobin >16.5 mg/dL) to boost oxygen-carrying capacity.
    -   Maladaptively, extreme polycythemia (eg, generally, hematocrit >60%) can cause a type of hyperviscosity syndrome in which vascular sludging produces neurologic symptoms (eg, headache, confusion), thrombosis, retinal edema, mucosal bleeding (eg, epistaxis), and heart failure.
-   **Angiogenesis**:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor, mainly in the heart and skeletal muscle.
    -   Adaptively, this promotes the formation of collateral circulation (eg, to bypass chronic coronary artery stenosis).
    -   Maladaptively, disorganized neovascularization (eg, diabetic proliferative retinopathy) results in fragile, hemorrhage-prone vessels.
-   **Anaerobic (glycolytic) shift**:  HIF1ɑ induces upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (eg, hexokinase), mainly in the heart and brain.
    -   Adaptively, this preserves ATP production despite low O<sub>2</sub> (eg, hibernating myocardium).
    -   Maladaptively, this results in several downstream changes, such as cellular proliferation (eg, Warburg effect in cancer cells, in which glucose is converted to lactate via aerobic glycolysis in the cytosol rather than being fully metabolized in the mitochondria, fueling rapid cell growth).  This shift also results in inflammation (eg, leukocyte activation due to glycolytic products).

## Vascular responses

Effects of hypoxia on vascular resistance are not dependent on HIF1ɑ.  Instead, vessels respond directly to O<sub>2</sub> itself, reactive oxygen species, or related metabolites.

-   **Systemic vasodilation**:  Hypoxia (eg, exercising skeletal muscle) stimulates the production of anaerobic metabolites such as adenosine, lactate, and nitric oxide that promote vasodilation.  Low O<sub>2</sub> tension directly relaxes vascular smooth muscle (eg, O<sub>2</sub>\-sensitive potassium and calcium channels).  These processes increase arterial perfusion to hypoxic tissue.
-   **Pulmonary vasoconstriction** ((Figure 13)):  Hypoxia is sensed by pulmonary arterioles, likely through mitochondrial redox potential, stimulating vasoconstriction.
    -   This is adaptive for short-term, regional hypoxia (eg, atelectatic lobe), because the selective vasoconstriction limits perfusion to poorly ventilated alveoli, maintaining V/Q matching.
    -   However, it is maladaptive for chronic, global hypoxia (eg, untreated obstructive sleep apnea) because whole-lung vasoconstriction can lead to pulmonary hypertension (eg, cor pulmonale, Group 3)

## Ventilatory response

Hypoxemia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies.  These chemoreceptors signal the medullary respiratory center to increase ventilation through deeper breaths and increased RR.  Hyperventilation has a much larger impact on lowering PaCO<sub>2</sub> than on raising PaO<sub>2</sub> ((Figure 14)).

-   **Ventilation**:  Hyperventilation causes an immediate reduction in PaCO<sub>2</sub> (respiratory alkalosis) because CO<sub>2</sub> elimination is directly proportional to minute ventilation.
-   **Oxygenation**:  Hyperventilation increases PaO<sub>2</sub> by only a small amount because perfusion to well-ventilated alveoli is already maximized, so further increases in ventilation do not significantly enhance O<sub>2</sub> uptake (ie, ceiling effect).  The hemoglobin in these regions is already near full saturation.

In other words, high V/Q areas (ie, hyperventilation) cannot compensate ((Figure 15)) for low V/Q units (eg, mismatch).  Breathing faster and harder will blow down CO<sub>2</sub> but does not improve oxygenation.

## Cell death

Severe or sustained hypoxemia can result in cell death, especially when combined with ischemia (eg, hypotension).  The dual insult of hypoxemia and hypotension is much more likely to cause tissue necrosis than either alone.  Tissue tolerance varies widely:  Kidneys (eg, acute tubular necrosis) can fully recover even after 15 minutes of complete circulatory arrest, whereas hypoxic-ischemic brain injury may be irreversible after just 3-5 minutes.

# Summary

Hypoxemia (PaO<sub>2</sub> <60 mm Hg) can be caused by 5 mechanisms:  low inspired oxygen (eg, high altitude), alveolar hypoventilation (eg, opioid-induced respiratory depression), ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch (eg, lobar pneumonia), diffusion limitation (eg, interstitial lung disease), and right-to-left shunting (eg, atrial septal defect).  The alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient assesses oxygen exchange across the alveolar capillary membrane and helps to identify the underlying mechanism.  Hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient is due to low inspired oxygen or alveolar hypoventilation (ie, high PaCO<sub>2</sub>).  Hypoxemia with an elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  A poor response to 100% supplemental oxygen suggests shunt physiology.

# Pulmonary Physiology: Gas Exchange # Introduction Respiratory gas exchange involves the following processes: - Oxygenation (oxygen extraction in the lungs). - Ventilation (carbon dioxide elimination by the lungs). - Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport in the blood. - Respiratory quotient (carbon dioxide produced per oxygen consumed). This article discusses these processes, how they are regulated at rest, and how they respond during exercise. # Oxygenation Oxygenation refers to the extraction of oxygen in the lungs.  Normal oxygenation requires: - Normal inspired oxygen (ie, PiO2). - Normal alveolar ventilation (ie, PaCO2), which requires normal minute ventilation and dead space. - Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (ie, A-a gradient), which requires: - Proper ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) matching. - Efficient diffusion. ## V/Q matching Ventilation (V) and perfusion (Q) matching can be conceptualized as the **opportunity** for oxygen uptake.  Wherever air (ventilation) is present, there should be corresponding blood flow (perfusion).  When ventilation is wasted on areas with insufficient blood flow (ie, dead space) or when perfusion is wasted on areas with insufficient ventilation (ie, shunt), V/Q mismatching occurs. Ventilation and perfusion both decrease from the lung bases to the lung apices ((Figure 1)): - Ventilation is slightly greater at the lung bases because basal alveoli, compressed by overlying lung weight, start smaller and can expand relatively more during inspiration; conversely, apical alveoli are already stretched open and expand less. - Perfusion is significantly greater at the lung bases due to the effect of gravity.  Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary arteries (PAs), allowing blood to flow continuously (because the PA blood pressure exceeds the alveolar air pressure).  At the apices, PA pressure falls below alveolar pressure; as a result, capillaries are compressed and perfusion is reduced. ## V/Q ratios Based on the relative pressures of the PAs, alveoli, and pulmonary veins, the lung is traditionally divided into 3 zones of West (named after physiologist John West) ((Figure 2)): - **Zone 1 (apices and upper lobes)**:  Ventilation is low at the apices because the already distended alveoli have limited capacity to expand further during inspiration.  Perfusion is even lower because hydrostatic PA pressure is reduced at the apices, allowing alveoli to compress the capillaries and limit blood flow (alveolar pressure > PA pressure).  As a result, the **V/Q is >1** (often >2).  This zone has a **dead space tendency** (ie, wasted ventilation) due to relative underperfusion. - **Zone 2 (midlung)**:  Ventilation is intermediate because the alveoli are moderately compressed and capable of further expansion during inspiration.  Perfusion is also intermediate because the increasing hydrostatic PA pressure toward the lung bases helps keep the capillaries from being compressed by alveolar pressure (PA pressure > alveolar pressure).  As a result, the **V/Q ~1**.  This zone has **ideal V/Q matching**. - **Zone 3 (bases and lower lobes)**:  Ventilation is high at the bases because the basal alveoli expand the most during inspiration.  Perfusion is even higher because the gravitational hydrostatic pressure in the PAs keeps the vessels open.  As a result, the **V/Q is <1**.  This zone has **shunt tendency** due to relative overperfusion. At **rest**, V/Q ratios normally range from 3 at the apices to ~0.6 at the bases, with a global average ratio of ~1 for the entire lung.  The spread of the V/Q ratios is often represented as a histogram centered at 1 ((Figure 3)). ## V/Q with exercise At rest, the V/Q ratio is ~3 at the apices, as described previously.  During exercise, a rise in cardiac output recruits the capillaries in the apices and upper lobes, increasing perfusion in these regions.  As a result, apical perfusion increases, lowering the V/Q ratio toward 1.  This enables V/Q matching to improve **even further** with exercise compared to at rest, optimizing oxygen uptake efficiency.  Consequently, a slight **increase** in PaO2 is considered a normal oxygenation response during exercise.  Desaturation is never normal. ## Diffusion Perfect V/Q matching brings air and blood into close proximity, but oxygenation is not complete unless oxygen effectively crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane, a process known as diffusion.  Normal diffusion is governed by Fick law ((Figure 4)).  The 2 most important variables in Fick laws of diffusion are the following: - Alveolar membrane **surface area (A)** determines the total area available for diffusion, with increased area increasing diffusion.  Membrane surface area is normally 100 m2 in a healthy adult (approximately the size of a tennis court).  It is reduced by conditions such as lung resection (eg, lobectomy) and emphysema. - Alveolar membrane **thickness (T)** determines the distance that oxygen needs to cross, with increased thickness decreasing diffusion.  Membrane thickness is normally 0.5 μm in a healthy adult and comprises 3 layers (epithelium, basement membrane, endothelium).  Thickness is increased by conditions such as interstitial lung disease and pulmonary edema. The other variables include the **diffusion coefficient (D)** (a unique value for each gas representing its solubility \[eg, highest for carbon dioxide\]) and **partial pressure difference (ΔP)** across the membrane (increased by altering the pressure or purity of inhaled gas). ## Diffusion with exercise Oxygen diffuses quickly enough to fully equilibrate between the alveoli and the capillary blood within the first third of the pulmonary capillary.  This rapid diffusion prevents hypoxemia during exercise (eg, even when blood flow triples).  Because diffusion reaches an early ceiling, oxygen uptake can be increased further only by greater perfusion.  As a result, in healthy individuals, oxygen uptake is said to be **perfusion limited**.  However, in individuals with alveolar membrane damage (eg, due to severe emphysema or interstitial lung disease), oxygenation can become diffusion limited ((Figure 5)).  Oxygenation might be marginally normal at rest, but significant desaturation can often be revealed by exertion. # Ventilation Ventilation refers to the elimination of carbon dioxide by the lungs.  It requires normal alveolar ventilation (VA).  Therefore, alveolar hypoventilation and hypercapnia (ie, PaCO2 >45 mm Hg) are synonymous. ## Minute ventilation Minute ventilation (VE) is the total respired volume per minute.  It is calculated as the product of tidal volume (VT) and respiratory rate (RR) (VE = VT · RR).  Normal VT is approximately 500 mL, and normal RR is 12/min, yielding a typical VE of 6 L/min. ## Alveolar ventilation Alveolar ventilation (VA) is the total respired volume that participates in alveolar gas exchange.  It is equal to VE **minus the dead space ventilation (V****D****)**.  Dead space is the fraction of VT that is unavailable for exchange.  There are 2 components of VD ((Figure 6)): - **Anatomic V****D** is created by the conducting airways, such as the trachea and bronchi, where no gas exchange occurs.  In adults, this is a fixed value of roughly 150 mL, so only 350 mL of a normal 500-mL VT ever reaches the alveoli.  As VT decreases, the anatomic dead space fraction increases ((Figure 7)).  For example, with a 300-mL VT, only 150 mL reaches the alveoli. - **Alveolar V****D** is created by alveoli with very high V/Q ratios (eg, extreme lung apices), where perfusion is low compared to ventilation.  Under normal conditions, alveolar dead space is minimal (eg, 5-10 mL), but it can be greatly increased by conditions that reduce perfusion (eg, pulmonary embolism). VA is calculated as VA = (VT − VD) · RR.  Therefore, in normal conditions, VA = (500 − 150) · 12 = 4.2 L/min.  A slower, deeper breathing pattern (eg, VT = 600 mL, RR = 10/min) is preferable to a faster, shallower one (eg, VT = 300 mL, RR = 20/min), even if VE is the same (eg, 6 L/min for both).  The shallow pattern results in a lower VA because more VT is wasted in anatomic dead space. ## PaCO2 PaCO2 is directly proportional to the carbon dioxide production rate (VCO2) and inversely proportional to VA (ie, PaCO2 ∝ VCO2 / VA): - VCO2 (ie, ventilatory load) is determined by metabolic rate.  It increases with exercise, pathologic conditions (eg, fever, hyperthyroidism, sepsis, burns, trauma), and overfeeding (especially with a carbohydrate-rich diet). - VA is determined by VE and dead space, as discussed previously. Normally, a rise in VCO2 is accompanied by a proportional rise in VA.  Peripheral and central chemoreceptors rapidly adjust ventilation to maintain arterial carbon dioxide within a normal range.  If VA fails to keep pace with VCO2, acute hypercapnic respiratory failure results.  This is seen in severe exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, when patients generate more carbon dioxide from their own work of breathing than they can expel through ventilation. ## Ventilation with exercise Exercise leads to increases in both VT and RR.  The respiratory response differs based on the presence of lung disease: - **Healthy**:  With exercise that is low-to-moderate intensity, **V****T** **increases first**.  With higher-intensity exercise, RR increases as VT approaches inspiratory capacity. - **Abnormal**:  In patients with lung disease or neuromuscular weakness, RR increases earlier and more sharply because VT cannot increase sufficiently. In other words, VT is the primary mechanism for increasing ventilation, whereas RR becomes more important as ventilatory load increases.  In clinical practice, persistent tachypnea at rest often signals a serious underlying illness. # Gas transport ## Oxygen transport Oxygen is transported in the blood in 2 forms: - Some 98.5% of oxygen is bound to hemoglobin **(HbO****2****)**.  Each gram of hemoglobin can carry **1.34** mL of oxygen when fully saturated (ie, SaO2 100%). - Some 1.5% of oxygen is carried as a dissolved gas in the plasma **(PaO****2****)**.  Only **0.003** mL of oxygen can dissolve in each deciliter of blood per every 1 mm Hg of increase in partial pressure. Total blood oxygen content (CaO2) is the sum of HbO2 and PaO2:

CaO2 = HbO2 + PaO2\= (1.34 · SaO2 · Hb) + (0.003 · PaO2)

In a healthy patient with normal hemoglobin (eg, Hb = 15 g/dL) and normal oxygenation (eg, SaO2 = 99%, PaO2 = 90 mm Hg), the oxygen carrying capacity is 20.1 mL O2/dL of blood. Carrying capacity is determined **almost entirely** by hemoglobin concentration.  For example, when a patient with severe anemia (eg, Hb = 5 mg/dL) is breathing pure oxygen (ie, SaO2 = 99%, PaO2 = 600 mm Hg), the oxygen-carrying capacity is only 8.43 mL O2/dL of blood (only 42% of normal).  Therefore, the total CaO2 remains very low despite maximizing the dissolved oxygen. ## Carbon dioxide transport Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood in 3 forms: - 70% of carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate anion **(HCO****3****−****)**. - 23% of carbon dioxide is transported as carbaminohemoglobin **(HbCO****2****)**. - 7% of carbon dioxide is carried as a dissolved gas in the plasma **(PaCO****2****)**. These 3 states are in an equilibrium mediated by **carbonic anhydrase** in red blood cells ((Figure 8)).  When PaCO2 increases, more HCO3− is formed and subsequently transported out of red blood cells in exchange for chloride anions to maintain electrical neutrality (ie, Hamburger phenomenon).  This phenomenon is one of the reasons that metabolic alkalosis (excess plasma HCO3−) is often accompanied by hypochloremia. Some of the carbon dioxide binds to the terminal amine group of hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin; when exposed to high levels of oxygen in the lungs, the hemoglobin releases carbon dioxide so that it can bind oxygen instead (ie, Haldane and Bohr effects) ((Figure 9)).  This phenomenon contributes to oxygen-induced hypercapnia in patients with marginal VA (sometimes called "chronic carbon dioxide retainers") who receive excessive supplemental oxygen ((Figure 10)). # Respiratory quotient The respiratory quotient (RQ), sometimes referred to as the respiratory exchange ratio, is the ratio between carbon dioxide production and oxygen consumption (RQ = VCO2 / VO2).  The RQ is mainly affected by dietary composition and exercise. ## Effect of dietary composition Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins have differing RQ levels: - The RQ of **carbohydrates** is ~1 because complete oxidation of glucose produces 6 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 6 molecules of oxygen (C6H12O6 + **6 O****2** → **6 CO****2** + 6 H2O + 32 ATP). - The RQ of **fats** is ~0.7 because complete oxidation of a long-chain fatty acid (eg, palmitic acid) produces ~16 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 23 molecules of oxygen (C16H32O2 + **23 O****2** → **16 CO****2** + 16 H2O + 106 ATP). - The RQ of **proteins** is ~0.85 because complete oxidation of amino acids through intermediate reactions (eg, gluconeogenesis) produces 5 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 6 molecules of oxygen (eg, alanine \[C3H7​NO2\] ​+ **6 O****2** → **5 CO****2** + 3 H2O + 15 ATP). For a normal Western diet, the **overall RQ is ~0.8**.  This value is used in the alveolar gas equation (PAO2 = PiO2 − PaCO2 / **RQ** = 150 − PaCO2 / **0.8**). Overfeeding with high-carbohydrate diets can increase RQ and contribute to worsening hypercapnia in patients with underlying respiratory failure.  Therefore, fat- and protein-rich diets are often preferred to help reduce RQ and assist with respiratory recovery (eg, ventilator weaning). ## Effect of exercise The RQ increases during exercise.  At rest or during routine activity, the RQ is approximately 0.8.  With more intense exercise, tissues preferentially use carbohydrates for fuel, causing the RQ to increase toward 1.  With very-high-intensity exercise, the RQ increases further and can exceed 1 as the anaerobic threshold is reached (ie, oxygen is no longer being consumed, but carbon dioxide is still being produced from glycolysis). # Summary Respiratory gas exchange encompasses the processes of oxygenation, ventilation, and gas transport in the blood. Effective oxygenation requires normal alveolar-capillary exchange.  It requires tight ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) matching (ie, opportunity for air to contact blood) and rapid diffusion across the alveolar membrane (ie, speed of oxygen uptake).  V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation leads to impaired alveolar-capillary exchange and a subsequent fall in PaO2 (ie, hypoxemia).  Blood oxygen content is mainly carried by hemoglobin (98.5%). Effective ventilation requires normal minute ventilation (tidal volume · respiratory rate) and minimal dead space volume.  Insufficient minute ventilation or abnormally increased dead space leads to alveolar hypoventilation and a subsequent rise in PaCO2 (ie, hypercapnia), which can also cause secondary hypoxemia.  Blood carbon dioxide content is mainly carried as intracellular bicarbonate in red blood cells (70%). ​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​
